subject: Introduction to Law
sourceRef: Introduction to Law — History and concepts
stem: Why is the Code of Hammurabi important in legal history?
choice1: It is one of the earliest written collections of rules.
choice2: It is the earliest known charter limiting a king's power.
choice3: It introduced binding precedent into English law.
choice4: It created the first permanent international court.
correctChoice: It is one of the earliest written collections of rules.
explanation: The Code is an early example of law set down in writing, listing roughly 282 rules on conduct and punishment. The near-miss describes a charter limiting royal power, which fits Magna Carta rather than Hammurabi.

subject: Introduction to Law
sourceRef: Introduction to Law — History and concepts
stem: What was the main influence of the Napoleonic Code of 1804?
choice1: It became a model for many later civil-law codes.
choice2: It became a model for many later common-law systems.
choice3: It replaced written codes with judge-made rules.
choice4: It made local custom rank above the constitution.
correctChoice: It became a model for many later civil-law codes.
explanation: The Code civil offered an organised, comprehensive text that many civil-law states copied. The common law spread through English institutions, not through the French code, so the near-miss names the wrong tradition.

subject: Introduction to Law
sourceRef: Introduction to Law — History and concepts
stem: The Nuremberg trials are most closely linked to the growth of which field?
choice1: International criminal law.
choice2: Private international law.
choice3: Domestic administrative law.
choice4: Customary property law.
correctChoice: International criminal law.
explanation: Nuremberg helped establish that individuals can be criminally responsible under international law. Private international law is a different subject: it decides which national law and which court apply to a cross-border private dispute.

subject: Introduction to Law
sourceRef: Introduction to Law — Definition of law
stem: Which statement best reflects a natural-law view?
choice1: Law should be linked to universal moral principles.
choice2: Law is valid only once a state body has enacted it.
choice3: Law and morality can never have any connection at all.
choice4: A rule becomes law only when a court applies it.
correctChoice: Law should be linked to universal moral principles.
explanation: Natural-law theories tie legal validity to moral principles drawn from reason or nature. The near-miss ties validity purely to enactment by the state, which is the positivist position.

subject: Introduction to Law
sourceRef: Introduction to Law — Definition of law
stem: Which statement best reflects legal positivism?
choice1: A rule can be legally valid even if it is morally bad.
choice2: A rule is legally valid only if it is morally sound.
choice3: Only long-standing custom can create binding law.
choice4: Validity depends on how popular the rule is.
correctChoice: A rule can be legally valid even if it is morally bad.
explanation: Positivism keeps two questions apart: whether a rule is law, and whether it is good. The near-miss makes moral soundness a condition of validity, which is the natural-law view.

subject: Introduction to Law
sourceRef: Introduction to Law — Definition of law
stem: Which feature most clearly separates law from personal preference?
choice1: It is backed by recognised authority and enforcement.
choice2: It matches the moral beliefs of every single person.
choice3: It stays the same for very long periods of time.
choice4: It deals only with relations between private people.
correctChoice: It is backed by recognised authority and enforcement.
explanation: Legal rules are made or recognised by authority and can be enforced by official bodies. Law does not need to match everyone's moral beliefs, and often does not.

subject: Introduction to Law
sourceRef: Introduction to Law — Definition of law
stem: Which is a central purpose of law?
choice1: To guide conduct, protect rights and settle disputes.
choice2: To replace all moral and social standards completely.
choice3: To turn every disagreement into a criminal case.
choice4: To stop legislatures from changing existing rules.
correctChoice: To guide conduct, protect rights and settle disputes.
explanation: Law sets standards, keeps order, settles disputes and protects rights. It sits alongside moral and social standards rather than replacing them.

subject: Introduction to Law
stem: Which description best defines a treaty?
choice1: A binding written agreement between states.
choice2: A binding written agreement between private firms.
choice3: A judgment given by a national trial court.
choice4: A scholar's explanation of an international rule.
correctChoice: A binding written agreement between states.
explanation: A treaty is a written agreement between states or international organisations, governed by international law. An agreement between private firms is a contract, governed by national law.

subject: Introduction to Law
sourceRef: Introduction to Law — Law and morality
stem: Which feature is more typical of morality than of law?
choice1: It usually grows over time without formal enactment.
choice2: It is usually changed by a vote in the legislature.
choice3: Breach of it always brings an official sanction.
choice4: It must be published before it can take effect.
correctChoice: It usually grows over time without formal enactment.
explanation: Moral standards develop gradually and need no law-making procedure. Change by legislative vote, official sanction and publication are all features of law.

subject: Introduction to Law
sourceRef: Introduction to Law — Law and morality
stem: Which feature is more typical of law than of morality?
choice1: Breaking it can lead to an official sanction.
choice2: Breaking it leads only to social disapproval.
choice3: It can never be deliberately changed by anyone.
choice4: It depends entirely on personal conscience.
correctChoice: Breaking it can lead to an official sanction.
explanation: Legal systems attach official consequences to breach. Social disapproval alone is the typical response to breaking a moral standard, so the near-miss describes morality.

subject: Introduction to Law
sourceRef: Introduction to Law — Hart and Fuller
stem: What was Hart's central position in the Hart-Fuller debate?
choice1: A rule can be valid law even if it is unjust.
choice2: A rule is law only if it meets eight inner criteria.
choice3: Only judges can decide whether a rule exists.
choice4: A rule becomes law after a moral referendum.
correctChoice: A rule can be valid law even if it is unjust.
explanation: Hart treated legal validity and moral merit as separate questions. The eight principles of law's inner morality are Fuller's, so the near-miss attributes Fuller's test to Hart.

subject: Introduction to Law
sourceRef: Introduction to Law — Hart and Fuller
stem: What was Fuller's central concern about law?
choice1: Law has an inner morality about how rules are made.
choice2: Law has no necessary connection with moral standards.
choice3: Law consists only of decisions made by judges.
choice4: Law is valid only when the public supports it.
correctChoice: Law has an inner morality about how rules are made.
explanation: Fuller argued that legality itself demands qualities such as clarity, publication, consistency and congruence. The near-miss states Hart's separation thesis instead.

subject: Introduction to Law
stem: A government keeps its rules secret, so citizens cannot read them. Which of Fuller's principles is most directly broken?
choice1: Promulgation.
choice2: Congruence.
choice3: Generality.
choice4: Constancy.
correctChoice: Promulgation.
explanation: Promulgation requires rules to be made public so people can know what is required. Congruence is a different failure: it concerns officials not acting in line with rules that have been published.

subject: Introduction to Law
stem: A new statute punishes conduct that was lawful when it was done. Which principle is most directly affected?
choice1: Non-retroactivity.
choice2: Non-contradiction.
choice3: Constancy.
choice4: Congruence.
correctChoice: Non-retroactivity.
explanation: Non-retroactivity means rules should govern future conduct, not reach back to punish past lawful acts. Non-contradiction concerns two rules clashing, which is not the problem here.

subject: Introduction to Law
stem: Two regulations are in force at the same time and require opposite actions in the same situation. Which principle do they breach most directly?
choice1: Non-contradiction.
choice2: Possibility of compliance.
choice3: Non-retroactivity.
choice4: Promulgation.
correctChoice: Non-contradiction.
explanation: The defect lies in the relationship between the two rules, so non-contradiction is the direct breach. Impossibility is the result; possibility of compliance is the principle used where a single rule demands something that cannot be done.

subject: Introduction to Law
stem: One rule orders every shop to be both open and closed at noon. What is the main legality problem?
choice1: Compliance is impossible.
choice2: Two rules contradict each other.
choice3: The rule is far too general.
choice4: The rule was never published.
correctChoice: Compliance is impossible.
explanation: A single rule demands the impossible, so the principle breached is possibility of compliance. Non-contradiction would be the answer if two separate rules clashed, which is not the case here.

subject: Introduction to Law
stem: Officials routinely ignore the rule they claim to be enforcing. Which principle is most directly undermined?
choice1: Congruence between action and rules.
choice2: Promulgation of the rules in force.
choice3: Generality of the legal language.
choice4: Non-retroactivity of legislation.
correctChoice: Congruence between action and rules.
explanation: Congruence requires official conduct to match the rules that have been announced. The rules here have been published, so promulgation is satisfied.

subject: Introduction to Law
stem: Rules are replaced every few days for no clear reason. Which principle is most affected?
choice1: Constancy, or relative stability.
choice2: Non-retroactivity of the new rule.
choice3: Possibility of compliance.
choice4: Promulgation.
correctChoice: Constancy, or relative stability.
explanation: Constant change stops people planning their conduct, which breaches the need for relative stability. Non-retroactivity would be the issue only if a new rule reached back to past conduct, which is not stated.

subject: Introduction to Law
stem: A regulation is worded so vaguely that ordinary readers cannot tell what it requires. Which principle is at issue?
choice1: Clarity.
choice2: Generality.
choice3: Congruence.
choice4: Constancy.
correctChoice: Clarity.
explanation: Clarity requires rules to communicate their demands in an understandable way. Generality is about whether a rule covers a class of cases, which is a separate question from how clearly it is written.

subject: Introduction to Law
stem: A decree is written to settle one named person's private dispute rather than to govern a class of cases. Which principle is weakened?
choice1: Generality.
choice2: Clarity.
choice3: Promulgation.
choice4: Non-retroactivity.
correctChoice: Generality.
explanation: Generality concerns rules framed for categories of conduct rather than one-off commands aimed at a single person or case.

subject: Introduction to Law
stem: What does a legal definition mainly do?
choice1: It sets out what is needed for a term to apply.
choice2: It sets out the punishment that a breach attracts.
choice3: It removes the need to prove the facts of a case.
choice4: It places one source of law above another.
correctChoice: It sets out what is needed for a term to apply.
explanation: A definition identifies the elements that give a term its legal meaning. Attaching a punishment is the job of a separate rule, which applies once the definition is satisfied.

subject: Introduction to Law
stem: Which statement is an obligation to do something?
choice1: Drivers must stop at a red light.
choice2: Drivers must not park on the pavement.
choice3: Visitors may enter the garden at noon.
choice4: A tenant has a right to quiet enjoyment.
correctChoice: Drivers must stop at a red light.
explanation: An obligation to do requires a positive act. The near-miss is also an obligation, but an obligation *not* to act, which is a prohibition.

subject: Introduction to Law
stem: Which statement is a prohibition?
choice1: No one may disclose the medical record.
choice2: The hospital must store it securely.
choice3: A patient may ask for a copy of it.
choice4: A patient has an interest in privacy.
correctChoice: No one may disclose the medical record.
explanation: A prohibition is an obligation not to perform an act. The near-miss is an obligation to act, which is the opposite type of duty.

subject: Introduction to Law
stem: Which statement best describes a permission?
choice1: Conduct is allowed, expressly or because no rule bans it.
choice2: Conduct is protected against interference by other people.
choice3: Conduct is required, and breach brings a sanction.
choice4: A higher rule cancels every lower rule at once.
correctChoice: Conduct is allowed, expressly or because no rule bans it.
explanation: A permission allows conduct, either expressly or through the absence of a prohibition. Protection against interference by others describes a right, not a permission.

subject: Introduction to Law
sourceRef: Introduction to Law — Rights and permissions
stem: Why is an exception to a prohibition usually called a permission rather than a right?
choice1: It allows conduct but need not create a protected claim.
choice2: It allows conduct and always creates a claim against others.
choice3: It requires another person to pay compensation.
choice4: It places the exception above the constitution.
correctChoice: It allows conduct but need not create a protected claim.
explanation: An exception lifts a ban in limited circumstances. It does not by itself give the holder an interest that can be enforced against other people, which is what a right does.

subject: Introduction to Law
sourceRef: Introduction to Law — Rights and permissions
stem: Which example is most clearly a legal right?
choice1: Freedom from torture.
choice2: An exception to a parking ban.
choice3: A suggestion in a textbook.
choice4: An unofficial local habit.
correctChoice: Freedom from torture.
explanation: A right is an interest protected by law. The parking exception is a permission: it allows conduct without protecting an interest against others.

subject: Introduction to Law
sourceRef: Introduction to Law — Rule of law
stem: What is the basic idea of the rule of law?
choice1: Public power is limited by law, not used arbitrarily.
choice2: Judges may set aside any statute they think unjust.
choice3: Government decisions never need legal reasons.
choice4: Only private persons must obey legal rules.
correctChoice: Public power is limited by law, not used arbitrarily.
explanation: The rule of law makes the state itself answerable to publicly known law. It does not give judges a free hand to disapply statutes they dislike; that would be arbitrary power in another form.

subject: Introduction to Law
sourceRef: Introduction to Law — Rule of law
stem: Which situation best supports the rule of law?
choice1: A minister's decision can be reviewed by a court.
choice2: A minister's decision is final and cannot be reviewed.
choice3: Unpublished rules are enforced against critics.
choice4: Officials are immune from all legal procedure.
correctChoice: A minister's decision can be reviewed by a court.
explanation: Independent review keeps government power inside legal limits. A decision beyond review is exactly what the rule of law guards against.

subject: Introduction to Law
sourceRef: Introduction to Law — Rule of law
stem: Which statement is inconsistent with the rule of law?
choice1: Senior officials are above the law while in office.
choice2: Senior officials are tried in the same courts as others.
choice3: Rules are published before they are enforced.
choice4: Government action can be challenged in court.
correctChoice: Senior officials are above the law while in office.
explanation: No person or office is automatically beyond legal accountability. The other three options all describe conditions the rule of law requires.

subject: Introduction to Law
stem: Who is a natural person in law?
choice1: A human being recognised as a legal subject.
choice2: An organisation recognised as a legal subject.
choice3: A citizen who owns registered property.
choice4: A court acting through its judges.
correctChoice: A human being recognised as a legal subject.
explanation: A natural person is a human being with legal personality. An organisation with legal personality is a *legal* (or juristic) person, which is the contrast being tested.

subject: Introduction to Law
stem: Which of these is normally a legal person rather than a natural person?
choice1: A registered company.
choice2: A company director.
choice3: A newborn child.
choice4: An individual employee.
correctChoice: A registered company.
explanation: A company has its own legal personality, separate from the human beings connected with it. A director is a natural person acting for the company.

subject: Introduction to Law
stem: A company breaks a contract that a director signed in the company's name. Who is normally the contracting party?
choice1: The company itself.
choice2: The director who signed.
choice3: All employees jointly.
choice4: The court hearing the case.
correctChoice: The company itself.
explanation: Separate legal personality means the company holds the rights and duties in its own name. The director signed as the company's representative and is not normally a party.

subject: Introduction to Law
sourceRef: Introduction to Law — Separation of powers
stem: Which branch normally makes and changes statutes?
choice1: The legislature.
choice2: The executive.
choice3: The judiciary.
choice4: The civil service.
correctChoice: The legislature.
explanation: Legislatures make and amend statutes. The executive may propose bills and issue delegated rules, but it does not enact primary legislation.

subject: Introduction to Law
sourceRef: Introduction to Law — Separation of powers
stem: Which branch mainly puts law and public policy into effect?
choice1: The executive.
choice2: The legislature.
choice3: The judiciary.
choice4: The electorate.
correctChoice: The executive.
explanation: The executive administers and implements the law that the legislature has made.

subject: Introduction to Law
sourceRef: Introduction to Law — Separation of powers
stem: Which branch settles legal disputes and interprets the law in cases?
choice1: The judiciary.
choice2: The executive.
choice3: The legislature.
choice4: The civil service.
correctChoice: The judiciary.
explanation: Courts decide cases and give authoritative rulings on what the law means.

subject: Introduction to Law
sourceRef: Introduction to Law — Separation of powers
stem: Why is the separation of powers valued in a democracy?
choice1: It stops one body from holding unchecked power.
choice2: It stops the branches from contacting each other.
choice3: It lets courts write all government regulations.
choice4: It gives the executive the final word on cases.
correctChoice: It stops one body from holding unchecked power.
explanation: Dividing public functions lets the branches check and balance one another. It does not require them to be isolated: they interact constantly, which is how checks actually work.

subject: Introduction to Law
sourceRef: Introduction to Law — Law and sanctions
stem: Which statement about legal sanctions is most accurate?
choice1: Official consequences attached to a breach of law.
choice2: Official consequences attached to immoral conduct.
choice3: Penalties that exist only in criminal law.
choice4: Imprisonment, in every area of the law.
correctChoice: Official consequences attached to a breach of law.
explanation: Sanctions are official legal consequences and take many forms across different fields. Immoral conduct that breaks no legal rule attracts no legal sanction.

subject: Introduction to Law
sourceRef: Introduction to Law — Law and change
stem: Why can law sometimes change faster than morality?
choice1: Authorised bodies can enact or amend rules at will.
choice2: Moral beliefs must be published before they change.
choice3: Courts have direct control over personal values.
choice4: Law needs no formal procedure of any kind.
correctChoice: Authorised bodies can enact or amend rules at will.
explanation: Law can be changed deliberately through recognised procedures, while moral attitudes shift gradually and without any formal act.

subject: Introduction to Law
sourceRef: Introduction to Law — Law and morality
stem: A community strongly disapproves of rude behaviour, but no legal rule forbids it. What follows?
choice1: It may be immoral in that community but still lawful.
choice2: It becomes a binding custom once disapproval is wide.
choice3: Moral disapproval creates criminal liability here.
choice4: A court must impose an official sanction for it.
correctChoice: It may be immoral in that community but still lawful.
explanation: Law and morality overlap but are not the same. Widespread disapproval creates neither a legal prohibition nor, on its own, a custom recognised as law.

subject: Introduction to Law
stem: Can one situation be governed by more than one legal rule?
choice1: Yes - rights, duties and fields of law can overlap.
choice2: Only when the rules come from different countries.
choice3: No - each situation has exactly one classification.
choice4: Only if the court refuses to decide the case.
correctChoice: Yes - rights, duties and fields of law can overlap.
explanation: A single event can raise contractual, employment, tort and criminal questions at the same time. Overlap does not depend on a foreign element.

subject: Introduction to Law
stem: Must every legally binding contract be signed?
choice1: No - some contracts are made orally or by conduct.
choice2: No - but only a court can create an oral contract.
choice3: Yes - a signature is always required.
choice4: Yes - unless the agreement concerns employment.
correctChoice: No - some contracts are made orally or by conduct.
explanation: Many agreements bind without a signed document, although particular types carry formal requirements. Courts do not create oral contracts; the parties do.

subject: Introduction to Law
stem: A customer orders a meal, pays the stated price and receives it. What is the best legal description?
choice1: Offer, acceptance and performance can form a contract.
choice2: No contract arises here, because nothing was ever signed.
choice3: Only criminal law governs this exchange.
choice4: It is a moral arrangement with no legal effect.
correctChoice: Offer, acceptance and performance can form a contract.
explanation: Everyday exchanges of goods or services for payment can form contracts without any written document.

subject: Introduction to Law
stem: What are the basic elements of agreement in contract law?
choice1: An offer and a matching acceptance.
choice2: An offer and a counter-offer.
choice3: A statute and a judicial precedent.
choice4: A right and a legal sanction.
correctChoice: An offer and a matching acceptance.
explanation: Agreement is formed by an offer and an acceptance that matches it. A counter-offer rejects the original offer, so it destroys agreement rather than completing it.

subject: Introduction to Law
stem: In common-law contract doctrine, what is consideration?
choice1: Something of value given in return for a promise.
choice2: Something of value given before any promise is made.
choice3: A judge's own view of what is fair.
choice4: A criminal penalty imposed for breach.
correctChoice: Something of value given in return for a promise.
explanation: Consideration is the value given in exchange for the other party's promise. Value given before the promise is past consideration, which is generally not good consideration.

subject: Introduction to Law
stem: One friend promises a gift and the other gives nothing in return. Under the basic common-law rule, what problem arises?
choice1: The promise may be unsupported by consideration.
choice2: The promise may be void for lack of capacity.
choice3: The promise automatically becomes a tort.
choice4: The promise creates international jurisdiction.
correctChoice: The promise may be unsupported by consideration.
explanation: A bare promise is traditionally unenforceable at common law because nothing was given in exchange. Capacity is a separate requirement and nothing in the facts puts it in doubt.

subject: Introduction to Law
stem: A seller tells a buyer the lowest price for a piece of land but never agrees to sell it. What is the main contract problem?
choice1: There may be no offer that could be accepted.
choice2: The price statement is an offer the buyer accepted.
choice3: Asking the price is itself a civil wrong.
choice4: Stating a price transfers ownership at once.
correctChoice: There may be no offer that could be accepted.
explanation: Giving a price supplies information; it does not show a willingness to be bound. Without an offer there is nothing for the buyer to accept.

subject: Introduction to Law
sourceRef: Introduction to Law — Contract and employment
stem: A person is hired to work for a business. Why may more than one field of law apply?
choice1: Contract and employment rules can both apply.
choice2: Employment rules replace all contract rules.
choice3: Only constitutional law governs paid work.
choice4: A situation can fall under only one field.
correctChoice: Contract and employment rules can both apply.
explanation: The job rests on an agreement but also attracts employment-law protections. Employment law adds to the contract rather than replacing it.

subject: Introduction to Law
stem: What is a tort?
choice1: A civil wrong that may give rise to a remedy.
choice2: A criminal wrong prosecuted by the public authorities.
choice3: A formal agreement between two states.
choice4: A rule that only a legislature can make.
correctChoice: A civil wrong that may give rise to a remedy.
explanation: Tort law deals with civil wrongs affecting interests such as the person, property, reputation or privacy. Prosecution by the state is the hallmark of a crime, not a tort.

subject: Introduction to Law
stem: What must a claimant usually show in a fault-based tort claim?
choice1: Intention or negligence, causation and harm.
choice2: Harm alone, with no need to prove any fault at all.
choice3: Offer, acceptance and consideration.
choice4: A treaty, a breach and a state party.
correctChoice: Intention or negligence, causation and harm.
explanation: Fault-based liability requires wrongful conduct, a causal link and damage. Liability on proof of harm alone is strict liability, which rests on a different basis.

subject: Introduction to Law
stem: What is vicarious liability?
choice1: Liability for another's tort because of their relationship.
choice2: Liability for one's own tort even where there was no fault.
choice3: Liability of employees for their employer's debts.
choice4: A criminal sentence imposed on a company's customer.
correctChoice: Liability for another's tort because of their relationship.
explanation: Vicarious liability attaches to one person for a wrong committed by another, typically an employer for an employee acting in the course of employment. Liability without fault for one's own act is strict liability.

subject: Introduction to Law
stem: What is the purpose of the 'reasonable person' standard?
choice1: It measures conduct against an objective standard.
choice2: It measures what this defendant actually intended.
choice3: It tests whether the claimant behaved morally.
choice4: It decides which of two treaties ranks higher.
correctChoice: It measures conduct against an objective standard.
explanation: The standard gives an objective benchmark for judging behaviour. What the particular defendant actually thought is a subjective question, which this test deliberately avoids.

subject: Introduction to Law
stem: What does strict liability generally mean?
choice1: Liability can arise without proof of fault.
choice2: Liability arises without proof of any element.
choice3: Liability arises only after an admission of intent.
choice4: Only criminal courts can impose this liability.
correctChoice: Liability can arise without proof of fault.
explanation: Strict liability removes the need to prove fault. Other requirements, such as causation and damage, still have to be established, so the near-miss goes too far.

subject: Introduction to Law
stem: Which description best fits criminal law?
choice1: It deals with conduct treated as a public wrong.
choice2: It deals with conduct that harms a private party.
choice3: It governs exchanges between two businesses.
choice4: It applies only where physical injury occurs.
correctChoice: It deals with conduct treated as a public wrong.
explanation: Criminal law prohibits conduct regarded as a wrong against the public interest. Conduct harming only a private party is normally dealt with by tort or contract.

subject: Introduction to Law
stem: Why is criminal law usually placed within public law?
choice1: The state normally brings the prosecution.
choice2: The victim normally brings the prosecution.
choice3: Every criminal case involves two companies.
choice4: Only international bodies can create offences.
correctChoice: The state normally brings the prosecution.
explanation: Criminal proceedings are an exercise of public authority against the accused. The victim is a witness, not the party bringing the case.

subject: Introduction to Law
stem: Which statement about criminal offences is accurate?
choice1: It covers serious violence and minor regulatory offences.
choice2: It covers serious violence but not regulatory offences.
choice3: Every breach of contract is also a criminal offence.
choice4: It never protects interests shared by the public.
correctChoice: It covers serious violence and minor regulatory offences.
explanation: Criminal law ranges from the most serious offences down to many minor regulatory ones, such as health and safety breaches.

subject: Introduction to Law
stem: A spectator watches a fight but gives no help or encouragement. What is the key question before treating him as an accomplice?
choice1: Whether the presence amounted to intentional encouragement.
choice2: Whether the spectator foresaw that a fight might happen.
choice3: Whether the spectator owns the nearby property.
choice4: Whether the fight took place under a written code.
correctChoice: Whether the presence amounted to intentional encouragement.
explanation: Complicity needs intentional assistance or encouragement; passive presence is not enough. Merely foreseeing that a fight might occur falls short of that intention.

subject: Introduction to Law
sourceRef: Introduction to Law — Branches of law
stem: What is public law mainly concerned with?
choice1: Relations involving the state and public power.
choice2: Relations between states and other states only.
choice3: Disputes between two private consumers.
choice4: The internal rules of private companies.
correctChoice: Relations involving the state and public power.
explanation: Public law covers constitutional, administrative and criminal law. Relations purely between states belong to public *international* law, a narrower field.

subject: Introduction to Law
sourceRef: Introduction to Law — Branches of law
stem: What is private law mainly concerned with?
choice1: Legal relations between private persons.
choice2: Legal relations between states and citizens.
choice3: Relations between states only.
choice4: The internal organisation of parliament.
correctChoice: Legal relations between private persons.
explanation: Private law covers contract, property and tort between private parties. Relations between the state and citizens belong to public law.

subject: Introduction to Law
sourceRef: Introduction to Law — Branches of law
stem: Which matter most clearly belongs to public international law?
choice1: A treaty dispute between two states.
choice2: A contract dispute between two firms abroad.
choice3: A boundary row between two neighbours.
choice4: An employee's pay under a local contract.
correctChoice: A treaty dispute between two states.
explanation: Public international law governs relations between states and international organisations. A cross-border dispute between private firms belongs to private international law.

subject: Introduction to Law
sourceRef: Introduction to Law — Branches of law
stem: Which issue is central to private international law?
choice1: Which country's law and courts govern a private dispute.
choice2: Which rules govern armed conflict between two states.
choice3: Whether a domestic offence deserves imprisonment.
choice4: Whether parliament followed its election timetable.
correctChoice: Which country's law and courts govern a private dispute.
explanation: Private international law deals with jurisdiction, applicable law, and recognition of judgments in cross-border private matters. Armed conflict is governed by public international law.

subject: Introduction to Law
sourceRef: Introduction to Law — Private international law
stem: A French buyer sues a Dutch seller over goods delivered in Belgium. Which question concerns jurisdiction?
choice1: Which court may hear the dispute?
choice2: Which country's law decides the dispute?
choice3: Will the judgment be enforced abroad?
choice4: Was the seller's conduct immoral?
correctChoice: Which court may hear the dispute?
explanation: Jurisdiction asks which court has authority to decide. The other two legal options are the applicable-law and the recognition questions, which come before and after jurisdiction respectively.

subject: Introduction to Law
sourceRef: Introduction to Law — Private international law
stem: In the same cross-border dispute, which question concerns the applicable law?
choice1: Which country's rules decide the issue?
choice2: Which court may hear the dispute?
choice3: Will another state enforce the judgment?
choice4: Which court building is easiest to reach?
correctChoice: Which country's rules decide the issue?
explanation: Applicable law identifies the legal system used to decide the merits. Which court may hear the case is the separate question of jurisdiction.

subject: Introduction to Law
sourceRef: Introduction to Law — Private international law
stem: What does recognition and enforcement deal with?
choice1: Whether another state will give effect to it.
choice2: Whether the court had power to hear the case.
choice3: Which country's rules decided the merits.
choice4: Whether the judge used an adversarial process.
correctChoice: Whether another state will give effect to it.
explanation: Recognition and enforcement concern whether a judgment already given will be accepted and carried out elsewhere. The first distractor is jurisdiction, the second applicable law.

subject: Introduction to Law
sourceRef: Introduction to Law — International criminal law
stem: When may the International Criminal Court become relevant?
choice1: A state is unwilling or unable genuinely to act.
choice2: A state has already tried the accused in good faith.
choice3: A local regulation is unclear.
choice4: A private contract lacks a signature.
correctChoice: A state is unwilling or unable genuinely to act.
explanation: Under complementarity, the ICC steps in only where the national system does not genuinely investigate or prosecute. A genuine national trial has the opposite effect: it keeps the case out of the ICC.

subject: Introduction to Law
sourceRef: Introduction to Law — International criminal law
stem: Which group lists crimes within the jurisdiction of the Rome Statute?
choice1: Genocide, crimes against humanity, war crimes, aggression.
choice2: Genocide, terrorism, piracy and international drug trafficking.
choice3: Negligence, trespass, defamation and nuisance.
choice4: Offer, acceptance, consideration and breach.
correctChoice: Genocide, crimes against humanity, war crimes, aggression.
explanation: The Rome Statute covers four core crimes. Terrorism, piracy and drug trafficking are serious international concerns but are not among them, which makes that option the near-miss.

subject: Introduction to Law
stem: Why does EU law not fit neatly into either public or private law?
choice1: It regulates both public bodies and private relations.
choice2: It regulates only the relations between the member states.
choice3: It contains no legally binding sources.
choice4: It is based entirely on unwritten custom.
correctChoice: It regulates both public bodies and private relations.
explanation: EU law covers institutional powers and competences on the one hand, and consumer, data-protection and contract rules on the other.

subject: Introduction to Law
stem: Which is an example of EU law affecting private interests?
choice1: Rules on how firms handle personal data.
choice2: Rules on how states vote in the Council.
choice3: Rules on declaring war on another state.
choice4: A purely moral duty owed between friends.
correctChoice: Rules on how firms handle personal data.
explanation: Data-protection rules govern how organisations process individuals' data, which is a private relationship. Council voting rules are institutional, and so a public-law matter.

subject: Introduction to Law
stem: Which measure is normally secondary EU legislation?
choice1: A regulation adopted under the treaties.
choice2: A founding treaty of the European Union.
choice3: A constitution of a non-member state.
choice4: A local custom followed in one village.
correctChoice: A regulation adopted under the treaties.
explanation: Regulations, directives and decisions are secondary acts adopted under the treaties. The founding treaties themselves are primary law, so the near-miss inverts the hierarchy.

subject: Introduction to Law
stem: Which matter is an example of EU private international law?
choice1: Recognising civil judgments across member states.
choice2: Defining genocide before an international criminal court.
choice3: Setting the rules for national elections.
choice4: Fixing criminal sentences in one town.
correctChoice: Recognising civil judgments across member states.
explanation: Instruments such as the Brussels regime deal with jurisdiction and the recognition of judgments in cross-border civil matters.

subject: Introduction to Law
stem: What does legal taxonomy do?
choice1: It sorts law into fields to locate an issue.
choice2: It ensures that fields of law never overlap.
choice3: It makes secondary sources legally binding.
choice4: It decides a case without using the facts.
correctChoice: It sorts law into fields to locate an issue.
explanation: Taxonomy organises areas of law so an issue can be placed. It does not prevent overlap: one set of facts can fall under several fields at once.

subject: Introduction to Law
sourceRef: Introduction to Law — Branches of law
stem: A citizen challenges a ministry's licensing decision. Which field is most directly involved?
choice1: Administrative law.
choice2: Constitutional law.
choice3: Contract law.
choice4: Private international law.
correctChoice: Administrative law.
explanation: Administrative law governs the legality of decisions taken by public administrative bodies. Constitutional law deals with the structure and powers of the state itself, a level above the individual licence.

subject: Introduction to Law
sourceRef: Introduction to Law — Branches of law
stem: Two neighbours disagree about who owns a strip of land. Which field is most directly involved?
choice1: Private property law.
choice2: Public international law.
choice3: Criminal procedure.
choice4: EU institutional law.
correctChoice: Private property law.
explanation: Ownership disputes between private parties are property-law matters. Boundary disputes between *states* would raise public international law, which is the trap in the second option.

subject: Introduction to Law
sourceRef: Introduction to Law — Branches of law
stem: A buyer is injured by a product that was carelessly made. Which fields may overlap?
choice1: Contract and tort.
choice2: Contract and criminal law.
choice3: Tort and constitutional law.
choice4: Treaty and customary law.
correctChoice: Contract and tort.
explanation: The purchase creates contractual rights against the seller, while careless manufacture may found a tort claim. Criminal liability would need a specific offence, which the facts do not give.

subject: Introduction to Law
sourceRef: Introduction to Law — Branches of law
stem: A state prosecutes a factory for a safety offence. Why is this a public-law matter?
choice1: A public authority is enforcing an offence.
choice2: The factory is a company and not a person.
choice3: Safety rules can never create private rights.
choice4: All disputes involving business are public law.
correctChoice: A public authority is enforcing an offence.
explanation: What makes it public law is the exercise of public power through prosecution, not the identity of the accused. A company can be prosecuted just as an individual can.

subject: Introduction to Law
stem: Which arrangement is least likely, by itself, to be a legal contract?
choice1: Friends agree to meet for coffee.
choice2: A buyer pays the asking price for a laptop.
choice3: A firm hires a worker at an agreed wage.
choice4: A business accepts a paid order for work.
correctChoice: Friends agree to meet for coffee.
explanation: Ordinary social plans usually lack an intention to create legal relations. The other three are commercial exchanges where that intention is presumed.

subject: Introduction to Law
stem: An employee carelessly damages a customer's property while doing assigned work. Which doctrine may make the employer liable?
choice1: Vicarious liability.
choice2: Strict liability.
choice3: Lex posterior.
choice4: Consideration.
correctChoice: Vicarious liability.
explanation: Vicarious liability makes an employer answerable for an employee's tort committed in the course of employment. Strict liability is about liability without fault for one's *own* act, which is a different idea.

subject: Introduction to Law
stem: A person claims compensation for distress after a relative is injured. What is the safest conclusion?
choice1: Recovery is possible only if set conditions are met.
choice2: Recovery follows automatically once a relative is hurt.
choice3: Emotional harm is never recognised in tort.
choice4: The claim belongs to public international law.
correctChoice: Recovery is possible only if set conditions are met.
explanation: Some systems allow such claims, but only within defined limits. The near-miss removes those limits and so overstates the position.

subject: Introduction to Law
stem: A sign says: 'Residents may park here after 18:00.' What kind of rule is this?
choice1: A permission that applies under a condition.
choice2: A prohibition that applies before 18:00 only.
choice3: A definition of the term 'resident'.
choice4: A positive duty to park after 18:00.
correctChoice: A permission that applies under a condition.
explanation: The rule gives a class of people the freedom to act, subject to a stated condition. It creates no duty to park, and the time limit narrows the permission rather than turning it into a prohibition.

subject: Introduction to Law
stem: A regulation says: 'Food businesses must display allergy information.' What kind of rule is this?
choice1: A positive obligation: it requires an act.
choice2: A negative obligation: it forbids an act.
choice3: A permission to display the information.
choice4: A definition of 'allergy information'.
correctChoice: A positive obligation: it requires an act.
explanation: 'Must display' requires the business to do something, so the duty is positive. A negative obligation would tell the business what it must not do.

subject: Introduction to Law
stem: A rule says: 'Vehicles without a permit must not enter.' What kind of rule is this?
choice1: A prohibition: a duty not to act.
choice2: A positive duty to obtain a permit.
choice3: A permission for permit holders only.
choice4: A definition of 'vehicle without a permit'.
correctChoice: A prohibition: a duty not to act.
explanation: 'Must not enter' imposes a duty not to do something. The rule does not oblige anyone to obtain a permit, and it does not grant permit holders a right of entry; it only forbids entry without one.

subject: Introduction to Law
stem: What is a legal problem?
choice1: An open question that legal rules can settle.
choice2: A disputed fact that evidence can settle.
choice3: Any disagreement between two private parties.
choice4: A question a court has already decided.
correctChoice: An open question that legal rules can settle.
explanation: A legal problem is an open question answered by finding and applying legal rules. A purely factual dispute is settled by evidence, not by legal analysis.

subject: Introduction to Law
stem: Which facts in a case are legally relevant?
choice1: Those that affect whether the elements are met.
choice2: Those that a witness can prove with evidence.
choice3: Those that support the client's preferred outcome.
choice4: Those that both parties agree actually happened.
correctChoice: Those that affect whether the elements are met.
explanation: Relevance depends on the rule: a fact matters if it helps satisfy or defeat an element. A fact can be easy to prove, or agreed by both sides, and still be legally irrelevant.

subject: Introduction to Law
stem: Why must factual claims be backed by evidence?
choice1: Because a court must be shown that the events happened.
choice2: Because a court must be shown what the rule means.
choice3: Because evidence makes a secondary source binding.
choice4: Because evidence decides which statute ranks higher.
correctChoice: Because a court must be shown that the events happened.
explanation: Evidence proves what happened. What a rule means, and whether it covers those events, is settled by argument and interpretation, not by evidence.

subject: Introduction to Law
stem: You have picked out the important facts of a problem. What normally comes next?
choice1: Name the legal issue, then find the law that applies.
choice2: Decide the likely outcome, then look for support.
choice3: Write the conclusion before reading any authority.
choice4: Treat each disputed fact as a separate offence.
correctChoice: Name the legal issue, then find the law that applies.
explanation: Analysis runs facts, issue, rule, application, conclusion. Deciding the answer first and then hunting for authority reverses the process and hides contrary rules.

subject: Introduction to Law
stem: What does 'facts need evidence, law needs argument' mean?
choice1: Events must be proved; rules must be interpreted.
choice2: Rules must be proved; events must be interpreted.
choice3: Facts are never disputed, but the law always is.
choice4: Proving facts and arguing law are the same task.
correctChoice: Events must be proved; rules must be interpreted.
explanation: Evidence shows what happened; argument shows what the rule means and how it applies. The second option reverses the two: you cannot prove the meaning of a rule with evidence.

subject: Introduction to Law
sourceRef: Introduction to Law — Conditions in rules
stem: A benefit is available if a person is under 18 or is a full-time student. What kind of conditions are these?
choice1: Alternative: either one is enough.
choice2: Cumulative: both must be met.
choice3: Hierarchical: the first one ranks higher.
choice4: Retrospective: they apply to past claims.
correctChoice: Alternative: either one is enough.
explanation: 'Or' means satisfying either branch is enough. 'And' would make the conditions cumulative, so that both would have to be met.

subject: Introduction to Law
sourceRef: Introduction to Law — Conditions in rules
stem: A licence requires an application form and payment of a fee. What kind of conditions are these?
choice1: Cumulative: both must be met.
choice2: Alternative: either one is enough.
choice3: Conditional: the fee depends on the form.
choice4: Specialis: the fee rule is the narrower one.
correctChoice: Cumulative: both must be met.
explanation: 'And' links the two requirements, so both must be satisfied. With 'or' they would be alternatives and either one would do.

subject: Introduction to Law
sourceRef: Introduction to Law — Conditions in rules
stem: A rule applies when a person enters without permission and intends to steal. Nadia entered without permission but had no intention to steal. Is the rule satisfied?
choice1: No: every element of a cumulative rule is needed.
choice2: Yes: intention is presumed once entry is proved.
choice3: Yes: the more serious element has been satisfied.
choice4: No: cumulative rules cannot create offences.
correctChoice: No: every element of a cumulative rule is needed.
explanation: Cumulative conditions are joined by 'and', so all of them must be present. Intention is a separate element that must be shown; it is not presumed from the entry.

subject: Introduction to Law
sourceRef: Introduction to Law — Conditions in rules
stem: A discount applies to seniors or registered students. Dara is a registered student but is not a senior. Does the rule cover Dara?
choice1: Yes: meeting one branch is enough.
choice2: No: both branches must be met.
choice3: No: the narrower branch takes priority.
choice4: Yes, but only if the rule is written.
correctChoice: Yes: meeting one branch is enough.
explanation: The branches are joined by 'or', so satisfying either one suffices. Nothing requires both, and specificity does not come into it.

subject: Introduction to Law
stem: What does HIRAC stand for?
choice1: Heading, Issue, Rule, Application, Conclusion.
choice2: Heading, Issue, Research, Argument, Conclusion.
choice3: Hearing, Issue, Rule, Appeal, Conclusion.
choice4: Hierarchy, Issue, Rule, Authority, Case.
correctChoice: Heading, Issue, Rule, Application, Conclusion.
explanation: The fourth stage is Application: testing the rule against the facts. Research and argument are things you do, but they are not the named stages.

subject: Introduction to Law
stem: What should a HIRAC heading normally do?
choice1: Name the legal issue, often as a short question.
choice2: Give the answer to the legal issue in one line.
choice3: List the facts of the problem in time order.
choice4: Set out the authorities the section will cite.
correctChoice: Name the legal issue, often as a short question.
explanation: The heading flags the question the section will answer. Stating the answer belongs in the Conclusion, not in the heading.

subject: Introduction to Law
stem: What belongs in the Issue section?
choice1: The legal question or questions the facts raise.
choice2: The legal rule that will answer that question.
choice3: The remedy that the client would prefer to get.
choice4: A list of every source the writer consulted.
correctChoice: The legal question or questions the facts raise.
explanation: The Issue names what has to be decided. The rule that answers it belongs in the Rule section.

subject: Introduction to Law
stem: What belongs in the Rule section?
choice1: The applicable rule, its elements, and authority.
choice2: The applicable rule tested against the given facts.
choice3: The writer's view of why the result is fair.
choice4: Extra facts that the problem did not supply.
correctChoice: The applicable rule, its elements, and authority.
explanation: The Rule section states and explains the law, broken into elements, with authority. Testing the rule against the facts is Application, the next stage.

subject: Introduction to Law
stem: What is the main task in the Application section?
choice1: Test each element of the rule against the facts.
choice2: Set out each element of the rule in order.
choice3: Restate the facts without mentioning the rule.
choice4: Give a one-line answer to the legal issue.
correctChoice: Test each element of the rule against the facts.
explanation: Application matches facts to elements and weighs both sides. Merely listing the elements is still the Rule stage; a one-line answer is the Conclusion.

subject: Introduction to Law
stem: What should the Conclusion do?
choice1: Answer the issue on the basis of the analysis.
choice2: Answer the issue by citing a fresh authority.
choice3: Add the facts that were not analysed earlier.
choice4: Restate the rule and all of its elements.
correctChoice: Answer the issue on the basis of the analysis.
explanation: The conclusion answers the question using what has already been shown. New rules, authorities and facts should not appear here for the first time.

subject: Introduction to Law
stem: A problem raises two separate legal issues. What is the sensible approach?
choice1: Run a full HIRAC on each, then conclude overall.
choice2: Run one HIRAC, then conclude on each issue.
choice3: Deal only with the issue that is easier to answer.
choice4: Merge both issues into a single unnamed question.
correctChoice: Run a full HIRAC on each, then conclude overall.
explanation: Each issue needs its own rule and its own application, so the structure is repeated. One shared analysis cannot show which rule was tested against which facts.

subject: Introduction to Law
stem: Why should the Rule section split a rule into its elements?
choice1: So each element can later be tested separately.
choice2: So the weakest element can safely be left out.
choice3: So the rule no longer needs any authority cited.
choice4: So alternative conditions become cumulative ones.
correctChoice: So each element can later be tested separately.
explanation: Splitting the rule shows exactly what must be proved and makes the application precise. It does not change the nature of the conditions or remove the need for authority.

subject: Introduction to Law
stem: Which Application paragraph is the strongest?
choice1: It links facts to each element and meets counterarguments.
choice2: It links facts to each element and avoids counterarguments.
choice3: It sets out the rule twice and adds no factual detail.
choice4: It covers every background fact, relevant or not.
correctChoice: It links facts to each element and meets counterarguments.
explanation: Strong application does both things: it ties the facts to the elements and deals with the other side's best reading. Ignoring counterarguments weakens the analysis.

subject: Introduction to Law
stem: The facts can be read in two ways. What should the writer do?
choice1: Set out both readings and predict the likelier one.
choice2: Set out both readings and leave the question open.
choice3: Treat the doubt as proof that no rule applies here.
choice4: Leave out the reading that weakens the argument.
correctChoice: Set out both readings and predict the likelier one.
explanation: Acknowledging both readings is necessary, but the analysis must still say which one a court is likely to prefer, and why. Stopping at 'it is unclear' gives the reader no answer.

subject: Introduction to Law
stem: Where should the main point of a paragraph normally go?
choice1: In the first sentence, before the support.
choice2: In the last sentence, after the support.
choice3: In a footnote attached to the paragraph.
choice4: Nowhere: the reader should infer it.
correctChoice: In the first sentence, before the support.
explanation: Legal writing states the point first and then supports it, so the reader knows from the start what the paragraph is for. Saving the point for the end makes the reader wait.

subject: Introduction to Law
stem: What is the main aim of a legal argument?
choice1: To convince a reasonable reader that a result follows.
choice2: To convince a reasonable reader that a result is fair.
choice3: To show the writer's command of technical vocabulary.
choice4: To describe the dispute without taking a position.
correctChoice: To convince a reasonable reader that a result follows.
explanation: A legal argument shows that the conclusion follows from the law and the facts. Showing that a result is morally fair is not the same as showing it is legally supported.

subject: Introduction to Law
stem: What gives a legal argument its strength?
choice1: Authority, operative facts, and explained reasoning.
choice2: Authority, background facts, and strong conviction.
choice3: A long list of quotations from several textbooks.
choice4: A conclusion stated firmly and repeated often.
correctChoice: Authority, operative facts, and explained reasoning.
explanation: The argument must rest on authority, on the facts the rule makes relevant, and on reasoning linking the two. Background facts and the writer's confidence add nothing legally.

subject: Introduction to Law
stem: What are operative facts?
choice1: Facts that decide whether an element is met.
choice2: Facts that both parties accept as having happened.
choice3: Facts that make the story vivid for the reader.
choice4: Facts that a court records but does not rule on.
correctChoice: Facts that decide whether an element is met.
explanation: Operative facts are the ones the rule itself makes important. A fact can be agreed by everyone and still have no effect on any element.

subject: Introduction to Law
stem: What is signposting in legal writing?
choice1: Wording that shows the purpose and order of ideas.
choice2: Wording that shows the source and rank of a rule.
choice3: A rule that every heading must be a question.
choice4: A way of avoiding a clear final conclusion.
correctChoice: Wording that shows the purpose and order of ideas.
explanation: Signposts tell the reader what is coming and how the parts fit together. They concern structure, not where a rule comes from.

subject: Introduction to Law
stem: Which sentence is a purpose signpost?
choice1: This submission assesses whether the hotel is liable.
choice2: This submission is divided into three main parts.
choice3: Everybody accepts that the hotel acted wrongly here.
choice4: The law on hotel liability is unfair and outdated.
correctChoice: This submission assesses whether the hotel is liable.
explanation: A purpose signpost says what the text sets out to do. The second option is also a signpost, but it signals structure rather than purpose.

subject: Introduction to Law
stem: Which sentence is a structure signpost?
choice1: The argument proceeds in three parts, taken in turn.
choice2: The argument sets out to establish that Ana is liable.
choice3: There are several points that could be mentioned here.
choice4: In a short answer, no structure is really needed.
correctChoice: The argument proceeds in three parts, taken in turn.
explanation: A structure signpost previews the order of the analysis. The second option is a purpose signpost: it says what the argument aims to prove, not how it is organised.

subject: Introduction to Law
stem: Once the main legal question is identified, what should the rest of the argument do?
choice1: Stay directed at answering that single question.
choice2: Raise every related question the facts suggest.
choice3: Hold back the rule until the final paragraph.
choice4: Build mainly on the writer's own experience.
correctChoice: Stay directed at answering that single question.
explanation: The identified question gives the argument its focus, and everything that follows should serve it. Adding further questions spreads the analysis thin without answering anything.

subject: Introduction to Law
stem: What should the introduction to a legal argument normally give?
choice1: The purpose, the legal question, and the structure.
choice2: The purpose, the legal question, and the authority.
choice3: The full factual record in chronological order.
choice4: A further issue that the body will not address.
correctChoice: The purpose, the legal question, and the structure.
explanation: The introduction orients the reader: why the text exists, what it will answer, and how it will proceed. The authorities belong in the Rule section.

subject: Introduction to Law
stem: Which sentence best introduces a rule?
choice1: Article 6 lays down three conditions for the claim.
choice2: Article 6 is the strongest point in this claim.
choice3: Article 6 probably helps, in the writer's view.
choice4: Article 6 is clear and needs no further analysis.
correctChoice: Article 6 lays down three conditions for the claim.
explanation: A rule is introduced by naming the authority and stating what it requires. The other options give an opinion about the provision instead of its content.

subject: Introduction to Law
stem: Which sentence is a sequence signpost inside an Application section?
choice1: First, Rui knew of the risk; second, he did nothing.
choice2: In short, Rui knew of the risk and did nothing.
choice3: To conclude, a further fact must now be added.
choice4: No reasonable reader could possibly disagree here.
correctChoice: First, Rui knew of the risk; second, he did nothing.
explanation: 'First... second...' walks the reader through the elements one at a time. 'In short' summarises; it does not mark a sequence.

subject: Introduction to Law
sourceRef: Introduction to Law — Civil and common law
stem: Which feature is most associated with civil-law systems?
choice1: Comprehensive written codes are a central source.
choice2: Judicial precedent is the central binding source.
choice3: Juries decide every civil and criminal case.
choice4: Oral tradition replaces all written material.
correctChoice: Comprehensive written codes are a central source.
explanation: Civil-law systems organise the law through broad legislative codes. Binding precedent as the central source is the common-law feature, so the near-miss swaps the traditions.

subject: Introduction to Law
sourceRef: Introduction to Law — Civil and common law
stem: Which feature is most associated with common-law systems?
choice1: Judicial precedent plays a major role in reasoning.
choice2: A single general code supplies the starting point.
choice3: Courts may never refer to earlier decisions.
choice4: Only agencies are allowed to interpret the law.
correctChoice: Judicial precedent plays a major role in reasoning.
explanation: Common-law reasoning works outwards from decided cases. Starting from a general code is the civil-law method, which is the swap being tested.

subject: Introduction to Law
sourceRef: Introduction to Law — Civil and common law
stem: Which statement best captures a broad difference between the two traditions?
choice1: Civil law stresses codes; common law stresses cases.
choice2: Civil law stresses cases; common law stresses codes.
choice3: Civil law has courts; common law has none.
choice4: Common law protects rights; civil law only punishes.
correctChoice: Civil law stresses codes; common law stresses cases.
explanation: Both traditions use legislation and case law; the difference is one of emphasis. The near-miss states the contrast the wrong way round, and is the same length as the key.

subject: Introduction to Law
sourceRef: Introduction to Law — Civil and common law
stem: A judge begins with a detailed code and treats earlier cases mainly as guidance. Which tradition is more likely?
choice1: Civil law.
choice2: Common law.
choice3: Customary law.
choice4: Public international law.
correctChoice: Civil law.
explanation: Civil-law adjudication starts from the codified rule, with earlier decisions carrying practical but not formally binding weight.

subject: Introduction to Law
sourceRef: Introduction to Law — Civil and common law
stem: A lawyer argues that an earlier higher-court decision binds today's court because the facts and the legal issue match. Which tradition is shown?
choice1: Common law.
choice2: Civil law.
choice3: Treaty law.
choice4: Customary law.
correctChoice: Common law.
explanation: Binding precedent and reasoning by analogy from decided cases are defining features of common-law practice.

subject: Introduction to Law
sourceRef: Introduction to Law — Civil and common law
stem: Can a country combine civil-law and common-law features?
choice1: Yes - mixed legal systems exist.
choice2: Yes - but only for rules of procedure.
choice3: No - the two traditions never overlap.
choice4: Only international courts may combine them.
correctChoice: Yes - mixed legal systems exist.
explanation: Quebec, Louisiana, Scotland and South Africa all mix the traditions, and the mixture runs through substantive law, not just procedure.

subject: Introduction to Law
sourceRef: Introduction to Law — Civil and common law
stem: Why do many countries share the legal tradition of a former colonial power?
choice1: Colonial rule left behind institutions and legal forms.
choice2: International law obliges former colonies to keep them.
choice3: A legal tradition can change only by referendum.
choice4: Courts cannot function without foreign judges.
correctChoice: Colonial rule left behind institutions and legal forms.
explanation: Historical transplantation explains much of the global map of legal traditions. No rule of international law requires a former colony to keep the inherited system.

subject: Introduction to Law
sourceRef: Introduction to Law — Civil and common law
stem: Which advantage is usually claimed for the civil-law tradition?
choice1: Codes make the law easier to find and more predictable.
choice2: Case-by-case reasoning adapts quickly to new facts.
choice3: Judges may set aside legislation whenever facts change.
choice4: Juries decide questions of national policy directly.
correctChoice: Codes make the law easier to find and more predictable.
explanation: Accessibility and predictability are the standard arguments for codification. Flexible case-by-case development is a genuine advantage, but it is the one usually claimed for the *common law*, so that option is right about the merit and wrong about the tradition.

subject: Introduction to Law
sourceRef: Introduction to Law — Civil and common law
stem: Which advantage is usually claimed for the common-law tradition?
choice1: Case law can adapt gradually to new situations.
choice2: A single code makes the whole field easy to find.
choice3: It stops judges from developing legal principles.
choice4: It removes any need for statutes altogether.
correctChoice: Case law can adapt gradually to new situations.
explanation: Incremental development through decided cases lets the law respond to new facts. Having the field gathered in one accessible code is a real advantage, but it belongs to the civil-law tradition.

subject: Introduction to Law
sourceRef: Introduction to Law — Civil and common law
stem: Which is a possible disadvantage of a heavily codified system?
choice1: Broad codes may adapt slowly to new situations.
choice2: Broad codes make the law harder for the public to find.
choice3: Judges in such systems must always use juries.
choice4: No legal remedies are available under a code.
correctChoice: Broad codes may adapt slowly to new situations.
explanation: Stability is bought at some cost in flexibility. The near-miss reverses codification's best-known advantage: a code normally makes the law *easier* to find.

subject: Introduction to Law
sourceRef: Introduction to Law — Civil and common law
stem: Which is a possible disadvantage of an adversarial process?
choice1: A better-resourced party may present a stronger case.
choice2: The judge must investigate every fact of the case in person.
choice3: The parties play no part in presenting evidence.
choice4: Earlier cases can never influence the outcome.
correctChoice: A better-resourced party may present a stronger case.
explanation: Because the parties run the case, inequality of resources can affect the outcome. Judicial investigation of the facts describes the inquisitorial model instead.

subject: Introduction to Law
stem: What does stare decisis mean?
choice1: A court follows binding decisions made earlier.
choice2: A court follows the most recent decision made.
choice3: A later statute always defeats an earlier one.
choice4: A court must cite at least one leading textbook.
correctChoice: A court follows binding decisions made earlier.
explanation: Stare decisis means an earlier authoritative decision stands and governs later similar cases. What matters is the court's rank and the similarity of the issue, not which decision is newest.

subject: Introduction to Law
stem: When is a precedent most likely to bind a court?
choice1: It comes from a higher court on a like legal issue.
choice2: It is from a lower court within the same hierarchy.
choice3: It is a recent news report summarising a case.
choice4: It matches the judge's own view of the merits.
correctChoice: It comes from a higher court on a like legal issue.
explanation: Binding force runs downwards: a court is bound by itself or by courts above it, provided the legal issue and the material facts are close enough. A lower court never binds a higher one.

subject: Introduction to Law
stem: What is a binding precedent?
choice1: The rule of an earlier case a court must now follow.
choice2: The rule of an earlier case a court may now follow.
choice3: Any remark a judge made in an earlier judgment.
choice4: A lower court ruling that binds the courts above.
correctChoice: The rule of an earlier case a court must now follow.
explanation: 'Binding' means the court has no choice. If the court may follow it but need not, the precedent is persuasive rather than binding.

subject: Introduction to Law
stem: What is a persuasive precedent?
choice1: A decision a court may follow but need not follow.
choice2: A decision a court must follow in similar cases.
choice3: A court order addressed to one named person.
choice4: A statute that parliament has already repealed.
correctChoice: A decision a court may follow but need not follow.
explanation: Persuasive authority can influence the reasoning without creating a duty to follow it. If the court has no choice, the precedent is binding instead.

subject: Introduction to Law
stem: What does it mean to distinguish a case?
choice1: To show the precedent's facts differ in a material way.
choice2: To show the precedent's reasoning was simply wrong.
choice3: To hold that precedent has no force in any court.
choice4: To have the earlier judgment struck from the record.
correctChoice: To show the precedent's facts differ in a material way.
explanation: Distinguishing accepts the precedent but shows it does not reach the present facts. Saying the earlier decision was wrong is a different move, and a lower court cannot make it.

subject: Introduction to Law
stem: Two cases involve similar injuries but arise under different legal duties. What must the court check before using the earlier case?
choice1: Whether the legal issue, not just the facts, is alike.
choice2: Whether the injuries in the two cases are comparable.
choice3: Whether the earlier judgment was longer in length.
choice4: Whether the two claimants instructed the same firm.
correctChoice: Whether the legal issue, not just the facts, is alike.
explanation: The injuries already look alike, so that similarity decides nothing. A precedent applies only where the legal question, here the duty in issue, is also sufficiently similar.

subject: Introduction to Law
stem: A lower common-law court thinks a higher court's ruling is wrong but cannot distinguish it. What should it do?
choice1: Follow the ruling, and may record its disagreement.
choice2: Depart from the ruling, and record its reasons.
choice3: Treat the ruling as a secondary, non-binding source.
choice4: Refer the ruling to a jury to be set aside.
correctChoice: Follow the ruling, and may record its disagreement.
explanation: Vertical stare decisis obliges the lower court to apply the higher court's decision even when it disagrees. It may voice criticism, but only a higher court can change the rule.

subject: Introduction to Law
sourceRef: Introduction to Law — Rights and remedies
stem: What is a writ?
choice1: A formal court order to do or stop doing something.
choice2: A formal statute ordering a court to hear a claim.
choice3: An informal request made by a lawyer.
choice4: A scholarly classification of legal fields.
correctChoice: A formal court order to do or stop doing something.
explanation: A writ is a formal judicial order linked to a particular remedy. It issues from the court; it is not an instruction given *to* the court by the legislature.

subject: Introduction to Law
sourceRef: Introduction to Law — Rights and remedies
stem: What does habeas corpus broadly protect?
choice1: It lets a detained person test the legality of detention.
choice2: It guarantees a trial by jury in every criminal prosecution.
choice3: It allows a company to avoid paying tax.
choice4: It lets a state set aside a treaty it signed.
correctChoice: It lets a detained person test the legality of detention.
explanation: Habeas corpus requires legal justification for detention and lets the detained person challenge it before a court. Jury trial is a separate protection.

subject: Introduction to Law
sourceRef: Introduction to Law — Rights and remedies
stem: What does the common-law phrase 'where there is a remedy, there is a right' emphasise?
choice1: Available remedies shaped which rights were recognised.
choice2: Recognised rights decided which remedies were available.
choice3: Rights exist only if written in a constitution.
choice4: Courts may never create any new remedy.
correctChoice: Available remedies shaped which rights were recognised.
explanation: At common law the available form of action came first, and the right followed from it. The near-miss runs the relationship the other way, which is the civil-law maxim.

subject: Introduction to Law
stem: What is the judge's usual role in an adversarial process?
choice1: A neutral umpire while the parties present their cases.
choice2: An active investigator who gathers the evidence himself.
choice3: An advocate for the weaker party in the case.
choice4: A legislator who writes rules during the trial.
correctChoice: A neutral umpire while the parties present their cases.
explanation: In the adversarial model the parties lead and the judge rules on fairness and outcome. Active investigation is the inquisitorial judge's role.

subject: Introduction to Law
stem: What is the judge's usual role in an inquisitorial process?
choice1: An active investigator who helps establish the facts.
choice2: A neutral umpire between the two opposing parties.
choice3: A passive observer while the jury runs the case.
choice4: A judge who accepts only prosecution evidence.
correctChoice: An active investigator who helps establish the facts.
explanation: The inquisitorial judge takes responsibility for directing the factual inquiry. The neutral-umpire description belongs to the adversarial model.

subject: Introduction to Law
stem: Which feature is typical of an adversarial system?
choice1: The parties largely control the evidence and argument.
choice2: The court largely controls the evidence and argument.
choice3: The represented party automatically wins the case.
choice4: Public opinion replaces the applicable legal rules.
correctChoice: The parties largely control the evidence and argument.
explanation: Adversarial proceedings are built around competing presentations by the parties. The near-miss transfers that control to the court, which is the inquisitorial arrangement.

subject: Introduction to Law
stem: Which aim is especially emphasised in the inquisitorial model?
choice1: Establishing the truth through judicial inquiry.
choice2: Establishing the truth through party competition.
choice3: Following precedent instead of hearing evidence.
choice4: Keeping the applicable rules unpublished.
correctChoice: Establishing the truth through judicial inquiry.
explanation: Both models aim at truth, but they differ on the route. The inquisitorial route is court-led inquiry; truth through competition between the parties is the adversarial theory.

subject: Introduction to Law
sourceRef: Introduction to Law — Judges and juries
stem: In which tradition are juries generally more common, especially in criminal cases?
choice1: Common law.
choice2: Civil law.
choice3: Customary law.
choice4: Treaty law.
correctChoice: Common law.
explanation: Lay jury participation in criminal trials is most closely associated with common-law procedure.

subject: Introduction to Law
sourceRef: Introduction to Law — Judges and juries
stem: In a jury trial, who normally decides whether the accused did the acts alleged?
choice1: The jury.
choice2: The judge.
choice3: The legislature.
choice4: The prosecutor.
correctChoice: The jury.
explanation: The jury finds the facts; the judge rules on the law and manages the trial. The near-miss swaps these two roles.

subject: Introduction to Law
sourceRef: Introduction to Law — Civil and common law
stem: A court questions witnesses itself and orders further evidence to clarify what happened. Which model is this?
choice1: Inquisitorial.
choice2: Adversarial.
choice3: Purely legislative.
choice4: Private international.
correctChoice: Inquisitorial.
explanation: Active judicial investigation of the facts is the defining feature of an inquisitorial process.

subject: Introduction to Law
sourceRef: Introduction to Law — Civil and common law
stem: The lawyers choose the witnesses, test each other's evidence and try to persuade a neutral judge. Which model is this?
choice1: Adversarial.
choice2: Inquisitorial.
choice3: Administrative.
choice4: Customary.
correctChoice: Adversarial.
explanation: Party-led presentation before a neutral decision-maker is the adversarial model.

subject: Introduction to Law
sourceRef: Introduction to Law — Rule of law
stem: Which set of features best reflects the rule of law?
choice1: Clear, stable, prospective rules and independent courts.
choice2: Clear, stable rules applied by the government itself.
choice3: Secret rules, wide discretion and retroactive punishment.
choice4: Oral commands that change daily and bind only outsiders.
correctChoice: Clear, stable, prospective rules and independent courts.
explanation: The rule of law needs both good-quality rules and independent adjudication. The near-miss keeps the rule-quality half but drops independence, leaving the government to judge its own case.

subject: Introduction to Law
sourceRef: Introduction to Law — Sources of law
stem: What does 'source of law' mean?
choice1: The recognised origin or form that legal rules take.
choice2: The recognised body that enforces the legal rules.
choice3: The reason that makes a party wish to go to court.
choice4: The building in which the court actually sits.
correctChoice: The recognised origin or form that legal rules take.
explanation: A source of law is where a rule comes from: legislation, case law, custom, treaties. Which institution enforces the rule is a separate question.

subject: Introduction to Law
sourceRef: Introduction to Law — Sources of law
stem: What is a primary legal source?
choice1: A text that contains the law or an official ruling.
choice2: A text that explains the law in an official guide.
choice3: A student's written summary of a class session.
choice4: A newspaper's account of yesterday's judgment.
correctChoice: A text that contains the law or an official ruling.
