correctChoice: Yes: consideration must be sufficient in law but need not be adequate in value.
explanation: Sufficiency means the counter-performance must have some value recognised by law. Adequacy, meaning economic equivalence, is not required: the courts do not police whether the bargain was a good one.

subject: Private Law
stem: B repairs A's roof for free. Afterwards A promises to pay B 200 euros for the work. Is that promise supported by consideration?
choice1: No: the work was already done, so nothing was given in return for the promise.
choice2: No: the work was done for free, so B never intended to create legal relations.
choice3: Yes: A received a real benefit from the work that B carried out on the roof.
choice4: Yes, as long as the sum promised is in proportion to the work that was done.
correctChoice: No: the work was already done, so nothing was given in return for the promise.
explanation: Consideration must be given in exchange for the promise. Here the act came first, so it is past consideration and the later promise is unsupported. The defect is in the consideration, not in the intention.

subject: Private Law
stem: A party is already bound by contract to do a job and asks for extra money to do exactly that job. Is the promise of extra money supported by consideration?
choice1: No: doing what you already owe is not consideration; something extra is needed.
choice2: No: a contract may never be varied once the parties have agreed its terms.
choice3: Yes: the other side gets the performance that it actually wanted to receive.
choice4: Yes: the parties freely agreed the new price, which is enough in itself.
correctChoice: No: doing what you already owe is not consideration; something extra is needed.
explanation: Performing a pre-existing duty adds nothing new, so it cannot be consideration for a further promise. Contracts can of course be varied, but the variation needs something extra in return.

subject: Private Law
stem: A creditor agrees to take 600 euros in full settlement of a debt of 1,000 euros that is already due. Why is that agreement normally unsupported by consideration?
choice1: The debtor already owed the whole sum, so he gives nothing new in exchange.
choice2: The creditor already owed the whole sum, so she gives nothing new in exchange.
choice3: A debt can be reduced only by an order of a court or by a formal deed.
choice4: Part payment counts as a breach of the original contract between them.
correctChoice: The debtor already owed the whole sum, so he gives nothing new in exchange.
explanation: The debtor provides nothing extra, because the full amount was already owed. Without some additional element the creditor's promise to give up part of the debt has no consideration, although promissory estoppel may stop her going back on it.

subject: Private Law
stem: What is the difference between executory and executed consideration?
choice1: Executory is a promise of future performance; executed is given for an act done.
choice2: Executed is a promise of future performance; executory is given for an act done.
choice3: Executory applies to goods, while executed applies to the supply of services.
choice4: Executed is simply another name for consideration that is past consideration.
correctChoice: Executory is a promise of future performance; executed is given for an act done.
explanation: Executory consideration consists of promises still to be performed. Executed consideration is given in exchange for an act performed under the agreement. Neither is past consideration, which comes before the promise altogether.

subject: Private Law
stem: What is the main limit on the doctrine of promissory estoppel?
choice1: It can stop a right being enforced but cannot create a new cause of action.
choice2: It can create a new cause of action but cannot stop a right being enforced.
choice3: It applies only where the promise was recorded in a signed deed.
choice4: It applies only to promises made between members of the same family.
correctChoice: It can stop a right being enforced but cannot create a new cause of action.
explanation: Promissory estoppel needs an existing relationship, a clear promise not to enforce legal rights, reliance by the promisee to his detriment, and unfairness in going back on the promise. Even then it works as a shield, not a sword.

subject: Private Law
stem: How can a promise bind in English law without consideration?
choice1: By being made in a deed: in writing, signed and witnessed.
choice2: By being made in writing and signed before a public notary.
choice3: By being repeated in a second promise a short time later.
choice4: By being accepted in writing by the person who benefits.
correctChoice: By being made in a deed: in writing, signed and witnessed.
explanation: A gratuitous promise has no consideration, so English law requires the form of a deed. The notarial deed does a similar job in civil-law systems, but it is not what English law asks for.

subject: Private Law
stem: A promise is made for the benefit of a third party, who gave nothing in return and is not a party to the agreement. Can she enforce it at common law?
choice1: No: consideration must move from the person who wants to enforce the promise.
choice2: No: consideration must move to the person who wants to enforce the promise.
choice3: Yes: the promise was made for her benefit, which is enough to enforce it.
choice4: Yes, but only if the promisor still agrees when she brings the claim.
correctChoice: No: consideration must move from the person who wants to enforce the promise.
explanation: Under the traditional rule consideration must move from the promisee. Someone who gave nothing and is not a party cannot enforce the promise, although statutory reform and recognised exceptions have softened this.

subject: Private Law
stem: What does causa do in the legal systems that use it?
choice1: It identifies the aim of the contract and lets a court refuse effect if it fails.
choice2: It identifies the aim of the contract and checks the exchange is of equal value.
choice3: It decides which of the two parties has to perform its obligation first.
choice4: It decides which form the contract has to take in order to be valid.
correctChoice: It identifies the aim of the contract and lets a court refuse effect if it fails.
explanation: Causa supplies a reason for holding the parties bound. It can be seen objectively (what the contract achieves) or subjectively (the parties' motive) and allows a court to deny effect where the aim cannot be reached, for example where the subject matter does not exist. It does not test whether the exchange is equal.

subject: Private Law
stem: Which statement about consideration and causa is accurate?
choice1: Both answer which agreements deserve enforcement; some civil systems now use intention.
choice2: Both answer which agreements deserve enforcement; the common law now uses intention.
choice3: Causa belongs to the common law and consideration to the civil-law tradition.
choice4: Both are required in every modern European legal system without exception.
correctChoice: Both answer which agreements deserve enforcement; some civil systems now use intention.
explanation: Consideration and causa both answer the question raised by pacta sunt servanda: which agreements should the law enforce? In several civil-law systems causa has been dropped in favour of the requirement of an intention to be legally bound. The common law still requires consideration.

subject: Private Law
stem: Which statement about legal capacity is correct?
choice1: The rules protect people who may not be able to look after their own interests.
choice2: The rules punish those who contract with people unable to protect themselves.
choice3: A minor can never conclude any contract at all, in any circumstances.
choice4: Capacity, once gained at the age of majority, can never be lost again.
correctChoice: The rules protect people who may not be able to look after their own interests.
explanation: Incapacity is a protective device, not a sanction. It does not block every transaction by a minor, and capacity can be affected later in life by illness or disability.

subject: Private Law
stem: A contract is made by someone who lacks legal capacity. What is the usual consequence?
choice1: It is voidable, so the protected party may set it aside but is not forced to.
choice2: It is void, so neither of the two parties can derive any right from it.
choice3: It is unenforceable until the protected party reaches the age of majority.
choice4: It is valid and fully enforceable against both of the parties to it.
correctChoice: It is voidable, so the protected party may set it aside but is not forced to.
explanation: Contracts affected by incapacity can normally be set aside by the protected party or their legal representative, which is what 'voidable' means. The other party cannot demand performance, but the protected party may choose to keep the contract alive, which is why it is not simply void.

subject: Private Law
stem: A shop supplies goods to a sixteen-year-old and wants to be paid. When is the contract most likely to bind him?
choice1: If the goods were necessaries that suited his actual needs at the time.
choice2: If the goods were necessaries that suit someone of his age in general.
choice3: If he told the shop that he had already reached the age of majority.
choice4: If the goods were delivered before the shop demanded any payment.
correctChoice: If the goods were necessaries that suited his actual needs at the time.
explanation: Necessaries can bind a minor, but the goods must fit the minor's station in life and be genuinely needed at the moment of supply. Goods the minor is already adequately supplied with are not necessaries, however suitable they may be for that age group in general.

subject: Private Law
stem: Which contract made by a minor is most likely to bind him?
choice1: An apprenticeship contract that is, taken as a whole, for his benefit.
choice2: An apprenticeship contract that he says afterwards was good for him.
choice3: A trading contract he entered into in order to make a quick profit.
choice4: A guarantee he gave for money borrowed by one of his relatives.
correctChoice: An apprenticeship contract that is, taken as a whole, for his benefit.
explanation: Contracts of employment, training and apprenticeship bind where they are substantially for the minor's benefit, judged objectively. Trading contracts and guarantees do not, because they expose the minor to risk without a matching benefit.

subject: Private Law
stem: In a system where parental consent is decisive, a minor above the lower age threshold contracts without that consent. What is the position?
choice1: The contract waits for the legal representative's approval to take effect.
choice2: The contract is immediately void and no later approval can rescue it.
choice3: The contract is fully valid, because the minor is above the age threshold.
choice4: The contract binds the other party but never binds the minor himself.
correctChoice: The contract waits for the legal representative's approval to take effect.
explanation: Above the lower threshold a minor has limited capacity: the transaction needs authorisation and hangs in the balance until approval is given or refused. Below that threshold there is no capacity at all.

subject: Private Law
stem: Why may a minor's contract stand where he pays with money given to him for that very purpose?
choice1: Because he can then perform without suffering any economic disadvantage.
choice2: Because the money given to him transfers his parents' capacity to him.
choice3: Because the other party cannot be expected to ask about his means.
choice4: Because every transaction paid for in cash is valid whatever the age.
correctChoice: Because he can then perform without suffering any economic disadvantage.
explanation: The protection exists to stop minors taking on burdens they cannot carry. Where the minor is of an age for such a transaction and can perform it without economic harm, the contract stands. Capacity itself is not transferred by handing over money.

subject: Private Law
stem: An adult with an undiagnosed condition makes a contract. What must be shown for it to be set aside for incapacity?
choice1: That at the moment of contracting the condition prevented him forming a will.
choice2: That at the moment of contracting the other party knew about his condition.
choice3: That he has since been formally declared legally incapable by a court.
choice4: That the contract has turned out to be a bad deal for him in the end.
correctChoice: That at the moment of contracting the condition prevented him forming a will.
explanation: No formal declaration of incapacity is needed, but the threshold is high: the condition, even a temporary or undiagnosed one, must have been serious enough at that moment to stop a will being formed. What the other party knew is not the test.

subject: Private Law
stem: Why do some systems prefer assistance by a custodian to a full declaration of incapacity?
choice1: Because full incapacity also takes away freedom, so a graduated answer is better.
choice2: Because full incapacity makes the custodian personally liable for any losses.
choice3: Because declaring a person legally incapable is forbidden by the constitution.
choice4: Because assistance turns a voidable contract into a fully void one.
correctChoice: Because full incapacity also takes away freedom, so a graduated answer is better.
explanation: Declaring someone legally incapable protects them but also removes their freedom to act. Graduated measures let the person do some things alone and others with assistance, keeping as much autonomy as possible.

subject: Private Law
stem: A company concludes a deal outside the objects written in its constitution. How is this described?
choice1: The company acted ultra vires, that is, beyond the powers it was given.
choice2: The company acted ultra vires, that is, without any legal personality.
choice3: The company lacked capacity, because only natural persons may contract.
choice4: The company made a gratuitous promise, which is unenforceable as such.
correctChoice: The company acted ultra vires, that is, beyond the powers it was given.
explanation: A legal person normally has capacity, but it acts through representatives and within the objects set in its constitution. Going beyond those powers is ultra vires. The company still has legal personality.

subject: Private Law
stem: Why does the law require some contracts to be made in writing?
choice1: For cautionary, evidentiary, informative and protective reasons.
choice2: For cautionary, evidentiary, informative and fiscal reasons.
choice3: Because agreements that are not written down cannot be proved at all.
choice4: So that the parties can sign the agreement in front of a judge.
correctChoice: For cautionary, evidentiary, informative and protective reasons.
explanation: Form makes parties think twice (cautionary), secures proof (evidentiary), makes sure they know the consequences (information), and protects the weaker party (protection). Tax is not one of the four functions.

subject: Private Law
stem: A consumer credit agreement must be made in a prescribed written form. Which function does this mainly serve?
choice1: The cautionary function: it warns the consumer before a risky commitment.
choice2: The evidentiary function: it secures proof of what the parties agreed on.
choice3: The protective function: it keeps such deals for professional parties only.
choice4: The information function: it makes sure a lawyer advises the consumer.
correctChoice: The cautionary function: it warns the consumer before a risky commitment.
explanation: Where the point is to make a party stop and think before a serious financial step, the form serves the cautionary or warning function. Better proof is a side effect here, not the main purpose.

subject: Private Law
stem: A contract is valid without writing, but writing is needed in order to prove it. What follows?
choice1: The contract exists, and any adequate record, such as letters, may serve as proof.
choice2: The contract exists, but only a formal notarial document may serve as proof of it.
choice3: The contract does not exist until a formal document has been signed by both.
choice4: The contract exists but can never be enforced before a court of law.
correctChoice: The contract exists, and any adequate record, such as letters, may serve as proof.
explanation: Where the form is evidentiary and not constitutive, the contract is valid from the moment of agreement. The written evidence need not be a formal contract document: correspondence referring to the agreement may be enough.

subject: Private Law
stem: For which undertaking is a requirement of written evidence most often kept?
choice1: A promise to answer for the debt of another person.
choice2: A promise to repay one's own debt by instalments.
choice3: A contract to buy ordinary goods in a shop.
choice4: A contract of employment for an indefinite period.
correctChoice: A promise to answer for the debt of another person.
explanation: Of the old heads that required written evidence, the guarantee of someone else's debt is the one most widely kept, because the surety takes on a burden without receiving a direct benefit in return.

subject: Private Law
stem: Which transaction typically needs a notarial deed in the civil-law systems that use this form?
choice1: A promise to make a gift of substantial value.
choice2: A gift of substantial value handed over at once.
choice3: A sale of ordinary goods between two businesses.
choice4: A contract to supply services for a fixed term.
correctChoice: A promise to make a gift of substantial value.
explanation: The notarial deed is the strictest civil-law form and is kept for serious and infrequent acts: donations, mortgages, matrimonial property contracts, public wills and the creation of companies. A gift handed over immediately needs no deed.

subject: Private Law
stem: What does a notary do when a transaction must be made by notarial deed?
choice1: Draft the deed and confirm the parties mean to be bound after being warned.
choice2: Draft the deed and confirm the price agreed matches the value of the asset.
choice3: Register the transaction with the competent court so it can be enforced.
choice4: Decide whether each of the parties has the legal capacity to contract.
correctChoice: Draft the deed and confirm the parties mean to be bound after being warned.
explanation: The notary prepares the instrument and establishes that the parties, having been warned of the legal consequences, intend to be bound. This combines the cautionary and information functions in their strictest form. The notary does not value the asset.

subject: Private Law
stem: Why does handing over a present on the spot need no notarial deed, while a promise to make a gift usually does?
choice1: Because the transfer is already complete, so there is no promise to guard.
choice2: Because the person receiving it gives consideration by accepting the item.
choice3: Because gifts of movable property are free of all form requirements.
choice4: Because a completed gift can in any case be taken back at any time.
correctChoice: Because the transfer is already complete, so there is no promise to guard.
explanation: The form guards against binding yourself to a future gratuitous transfer, which is the dangerous step. Once the gift has been executed there is no such promise, so the warning function is unnecessary.

subject: Private Law
stem: In most civil-law systems a notary is needed to validate a land sale, but in at least one the notary's role is limited to registration. What is the effect in that system?
choice1: The sale is complete between the parties on agreement; the notary adds third-party effect.
choice2: The sale is complete between the parties on registration; the notary adds proof of the price.
choice3: The sale has no effect at all until the notary has registered it in the land register.
choice4: The sale is valid only once the full purchase price has actually been paid over.
correctChoice: The sale is complete between the parties on agreement; the notary adds third-party effect.
explanation: Where agreement on the asset and the price already transfers entitlement between the parties, the notary's intervention is about registration and effect against third parties, not about validity between the parties.

subject: Private Law
stem: What normally goes together with a pre-contractual duty to inform the consumer?
choice1: A right to withdraw within a short period after the contract is made.
choice2: A right to withdraw within a short period before the contract is made.
choice3: A duty on the consumer to give security for the price to be paid.
choice4: A ban on concluding that kind of contract by electronic means.
correctChoice: A right to withdraw within a short period after the contract is made.
explanation: Information duties are usually paired with a withdrawal right, often of one to two weeks after conclusion. The point is to give the consumer time to think it over and to inspect what was delivered.

subject: Private Law
stem: Which concern best explains consumer withdrawal rights in distance and doorstep selling?
choice1: The consumer may be taken by surprise or unable to inspect before agreeing.
choice2: The consumer may be unable to pay the price once the goods have arrived.
choice3: The consumer has no legal capacity to contract away from business premises.
choice4: The trader cannot be identified reliably in any electronic transaction.
correctChoice: The consumer may be taken by surprise or unable to inspect before agreeing.
explanation: Withdrawal rights answer pressure selling, artificially created needs, and the absence of any chance to examine the goods. They let the consumer think again after delivery. They are not about capacity or about ability to pay.

subject: Private Law
stem: Which statement about contracting by electronic means is most accurate?
choice1: Electronic form meets most writing requirements, but some types may be excepted.
choice2: Electronic form meets most writing requirements, but only between businesses.
choice3: Electronic form satisfies every writing requirement, with no exceptions at all.
choice4: Electronic form never satisfies a requirement that a contract be in writing.
correctChoice: Electronic form meets most writing requirements, but some types may be excepted.
explanation: Legal systems must make electronic contracting possible, but they may keep certain categories outside it, such as transactions in land or acts that need notarial or official involvement.

subject: Private Law
stem: A contract does not meet a required form. Which consequence is possible, depending on the system and the purpose of the form?
choice1: It may be void, unenforceable, or voidable by the party the form protects.
choice2: It may be void, unenforceable, or voidable by whichever party prefers that.
choice3: It is always void, in every system, whatever the purpose of the form was.
choice4: It stays valid, but the party at fault pays an administrative penalty.
correctChoice: It may be void, unenforceable, or voidable by the party the form protects.
explanation: Some systems declare the contract void, others treat it as unenforceable. Where the form exists to protect one party, the contract may be merely voidable, and then only that protected party chooses whether to keep it.

subject: Private Law
stem: Which circumstance may cure a failure to observe a required form?
choice1: Performance of the agreement, or reliance the complaining party caused.
choice2: Confirmation of the agreement in writing by the party who drafted it.
choice3: The passing of the limitation period without any claim being brought.
choice4: Registration of the agreement with the competent public authority.
correctChoice: Performance of the agreement, or reliance the complaining party caused.
explanation: The law may uphold an informally concluded contract in order to protect the very person the form was meant to help. Performance can cure the defect, and a party who made the other rely on the informal agreement may be barred from pointing to the missing form.

subject: Private Law
stem: How do form requirements relate to the principle of informality?
choice1: Informality is the rule, and form requirements are exceptions with a purpose.
choice2: Form is the rule, and informality is an exception for consumer contracts only.
choice3: The two belong to different branches of law and never meet in practice.
choice4: Informality applies only where the parties have expressly agreed on it.
correctChoice: Informality is the rule, and form requirements are exceptions with a purpose.
explanation: In principle a contract may be concluded in any way, which keeps everyday transactions workable. A form is imposed only where a cautionary, evidentiary, information or protection purpose justifies the exception.

subject: Private Law
subtopic: Common law and civil law compared
stem: Which comparison of the requirements for a binding agreement is accurate?
choice1: Common law: intention, agreement and consideration. Civil law: intention and agreement.
choice2: Common law: intention and agreement. Civil law: intention, agreement and consideration.
choice3: Both traditions require consideration, though each of them defines it differently.
choice4: Neither tradition requires an intention to create legal relations between parties.
correctChoice: Common law: intention, agreement and consideration. Civil law: intention and agreement.
explanation: Consideration is a common-law requirement. The civil codes compared have no equivalent, so agreement together with an intention to be legally bound is enough there.

subject: Private Law
stem: Which list of the elements of a binding contract is the most complete?
choice1: Offer, acceptance, intention, form where needed, capacity, no vitiating factors.
choice2: Offer, acceptance, intention, form where needed, capacity, fair terms on both sides.
choice3: Offer, acceptance, intention and capacity, which are the four general elements.
choice4: Offer, acceptance and consideration, which apply in every legal system.
correctChoice: Offer, acceptance, intention, form where needed, capacity, no vitiating factors.
explanation: The full checklist is agreement (offer and acceptance), intention, any required form, capacity, and the absence of vitiating factors. Fairness of the terms is not a general requirement, and consideration is added only in the common law.

subject: International Law
stem: How does modern constitutionalism differ from the older idea of limiting a ruler?
choice1: Public power itself must be created by law and limited by law, not only the ruler's conduct.
choice2: The ruler's conduct must be limited by law, but the source of public power stays political.
choice3: Public power may be used freely once the ruler has been chosen in a lawful way.
choice4: Every state must adopt one single written document that is called the constitution.
correctChoice: Public power itself must be created by law and limited by law, not only the ruler's conduct.
explanation: The older idea asked what a ruler may and may not do. The modern idea goes further: law creates public power and also limits it, so law decides who governs and how. Limiting conduct alone is the older idea.

subject: International Law
stem: Constitutionalism is best described as the ideal of a government that is:
choice1: created by law and limited by law, so that power cannot be used arbitrarily.
choice2: created by law but free to act in any way that serves the public good.
choice3: created by elections and limited only by the result of the next election.
choice4: created by custom and limited only by what the courts decide to allow.
correctChoice: created by law and limited by law, so that power cannot be used arbitrarily.
explanation: Both elements must be present: public power needs a legal source and legal limits. A good purpose does not remove the limits.

subject: International Law
stem: How are constitutional law and constitutionalism related?
choice1: Constitutional law is the law in the constitution through which constitutionalism is pursued.
choice2: Constitutionalism is the part of constitutional law that deals with the amendment rules.
choice3: Constitutional law exists only in states that have rejected the idea of constitutionalism.
choice4: Constitutionalism is a political idea with no connection to any legal rules.
correctChoice: Constitutional law is the law in the constitution through which constitutionalism is pursued.
explanation: Constitutionalism is the ideal of law-based, limited government. Constitutional law is the legal material that gives that ideal effect; it is not a sub-part of constitutionalism.

subject: International Law
sourceRef: International Law — What is a constitution
stem: What does a narrow understanding of the word 'constitution' refer to?
choice1: One or more documents with the special legal identity of setting out constitutional norms.
choice2: All rules that organise public power, including conventions, customs and daily practice.
choice3: Only those constitutional rules that a constitutional court has already interpreted.
choice4: Any statute that parliament adopts by a two-thirds majority, whatever its subject.
correctChoice: One or more documents with the special legal identity of setting out constitutional norms.
explanation: Narrow means a selected set of (almost always legal) documents. The option that adds conventions and practice describes the broad understanding.

subject: International Law
sourceRef: International Law — What is a constitution
stem: Which combination best shows a broad understanding of a constitution?
choice1: The written constitutional text together with conventions, customs and settled practice.
choice2: The written constitutional text together with every ordinary statute adopted by parliament.
choice3: Only those documents that carry the special legal identity of being 'the constitution'.
choice4: Only the judgments of the highest court, because that court always has the final word.
correctChoice: The written constitutional text together with conventions, customs and settled practice.
explanation: A broad understanding covers all norms that organise public power: de jure norms from the text plus de facto norms from practice. Limiting it to the formal documents is the narrow view.

subject: International Law
subtopic: De jure and de facto norms
sourceRef: International Law — What is a constitution
stem: What is the difference between de jure and de facto constitutional norms?
choice1: De jure norms come from formal legal text; de facto norms are followed in practice without being enacted.
choice2: De facto norms come from formal legal text; de jure norms are followed in practice without being enacted.
choice3: De jure norms bind the executive, while de facto norms bind only the courts.
choice4: De jure norms are made by parliament, while de facto norms are made by judges.
correctChoice: De jure norms come from formal legal text; de facto norms are followed in practice without being enacted.
explanation: De jure norms rest on formal law and text. De facto norms are not formally law, but people rely on them because they are consistently observed. One wrong option simply swaps the two labels.

subject: International Law
sourceRef: International Law — Features of a constitution
stem: What does it mean to say that a constitution is codified?
choice1: A document carries the legal identity of being the constitution of that state.
choice2: Every constitutional rule of that state is written in that document and nowhere else.
choice3: The state belongs to the civil-law family rather than to the common-law family.
choice4: The document can be changed only by a referendum of the whole electorate.
correctChoice: A document carries the legal identity of being the constitution of that state.
explanation: Codification means a document is legally identified as 'the Constitution of' the state. It does not mean the document holds every constitutional norm, and it says nothing about the legal family.

subject: International Law
sourceRef: International Law — Features of a constitution
stem: Which statement about codified and uncodified constitutions is correct?
choice1: Codification is a separate question from whether the state is civil law or common law.
choice2: Codified constitutions belong to civil-law states and uncodified ones to common-law states.
choice3: A state with an uncodified constitution has no constitutional law to apply.
choice4: An uncodified constitution can never be enforced by a court of law.
correctChoice: Codification is a separate question from whether the state is civil law or common law.
explanation: The codified/uncodified distinction does not match the civil-law/common-law distinction, even though the pairing looks plausible. A state with no single document can still be fully constitutional.

subject: International Law
sourceRef: International Law — Features of a constitution
stem: A state has no single document called its constitution, but its public power is organised and limited by law. How is it best described?
choice1: A constitutional state with an uncodified constitution.
choice2: A state with a codified constitution split over several laws.
choice3: A state with no constitution and so no constitutional law.
choice4: A state whose constitution is made only of court precedent.
correctChoice: A constitutional state with an uncodified constitution.
explanation: Codification means one document has the legal identity of 'the constitution'. Without it the constitution is uncodified, but the state still has a constitution and constitutionalism.

subject: International Law
stem: Which amendment procedure is the clearest example of rigidity?
choice1: A two-thirds majority in parliament plus approval in a referendum.
choice2: A simple majority in parliament, repeated after a one-month delay.
choice3: A new reading of the existing text given by the highest court.
choice4: A decision of parliament confirmed by the head of state's signature.
correctChoice: A two-thirds majority in parliament plus approval in a referendum.
explanation: Rigidity comes from demanding requirements: unamendable clauses, supermajorities or compulsory referenda. Simple majorities, waiting periods and reinterpretation are signs of flexibility.

subject: International Law
stem: What is the main benefit of a rigid amendment procedure?
choice1: Stability and continuity of the constitutional rules over time.
choice2: Quick adaptation of the rules when political circumstances change.
choice3: Certainty that the text will never need to be interpreted by judges.
choice4: Agreement between the constitution and the current parliamentary majority.
correctChoice: Stability and continuity of the constitutional rules over time.
explanation: Rigidity entrenches the constitution and makes institutions predictable. The price is less flexibility, which is the benefit of a flexible procedure instead.

subject: International Law
stem: A constitution needs a referendum to change the structure of the state, but other articles can be changed by an ordinary majority in parliament. This design is best called:
choice1: hybrid, because it mixes rigid and flexible elements.
choice2: rigid, because a referendum protects the core of the text.
choice3: flexible, because an ordinary majority is enough elsewhere.
choice4: unamendable, because different thresholds apply to parts.
correctChoice: hybrid, because it mixes rigid and flexible elements.
explanation: Demanding procedures for some matters and ordinary procedures for others produce both rigid and flexible features, so the correct label is hybrid rather than one of the two pure types.

subject: International Law
stem: What does constitutional supremacy mean?
choice1: The constitution is the highest norm, so all other law must conform to it to be valid.
choice2: The constitution is protected by a stricter amendment procedure than any ordinary statute.
choice3: The constitutional court ranks above every other institution of the state in the hierarchy.
choice4: The constitution prevails over the law of other states in disputes that cross borders.
correctChoice: The constitution is the highest norm, so all other law must conform to it to be valid.
explanation: Supremacy places the constitution at the top of the hierarchy of norms. The stricter amendment procedure is entrenchment, which protects supremacy but is not the same idea.

subject: International Law
stem: Which statement correctly separates a state from a nation?
choice1: A state is a political and legal community organised by a constitution; a nation is an ethnic or cultural community.
choice2: A state is an ethnic or cultural community; a nation is a political and legal community organised by a constitution.
choice3: A state exists only in international law, while a nation exists only inside domestic law.
choice4: A state and a nation mean the same thing when constitutional lawyers compare systems.
correctChoice: A state is a political and legal community organised by a constitution; a nation is an ethnic or cultural community.
explanation: The state is the legal and political community organised by a constitution; the nation is cultural or ethnic. One state may hold several nations, and a nation may cross borders. One wrong option reverses the two definitions.

subject: International Law
stem: Why is 'state' not simply another word for 'country'?
choice1: One state may contain several countries, with public power organised by a single constitution.
choice2: One country may contain several states, each one organised by its own separate constitution.
choice3: A country is a subject of international law, while a state exists only in domestic law.
choice4: A state must always be federal in structure, while a country must always be unitary.
correctChoice: One state may contain several countries, with public power organised by a single constitution.
explanation: A single state can contain more than one country; the United Kingdom is the usual illustration. The state is defined by the constitutional organisation of public power, not by geography.

subject: International Law
stem: How is 'the government' best defined in relation to the state?
choice1: The institutions and people who currently exercise the state's public power under the constitution.
choice2: The lasting political and legal community whose public power the constitution organises and limits.
choice3: The body that holds constituent power and may therefore adopt or replace a whole constitution.
choice4: The legislature, executive and judiciary taken together and treated as one single sovereign body.
correctChoice: The institutions and people who currently exercise the state's public power under the constitution.
explanation: The government is the current holder of public power. The lasting community organised by the constitution is the state itself, which is the near-miss here.

subject: International Law
stem: The authority to make a constitution is called:
choice1: constituent power, which is an exercise of sovereignty.
choice2: constituted power, which the constitution itself creates.
choice3: delegated power, which is used for the legislature.
choice4: residual power, which stays with the regional level.
correctChoice: constituent power, which is an exercise of sovereignty.
explanation: Constituent power creates the constitution and is an exercise of sovereignty. Powers created by the constitution are constituted powers exercised inside it.

subject: International Law
stem: A state refuses to let neighbouring states dictate how it governs its territory and population. Which dimension of sovereignty is in play?
choice1: External sovereignty: final authority in relation to other states.
choice2: Internal sovereignty: final authority inside the state itself.
choice3: Popular sovereignty: the people as the source of all authority.
choice4: Parliamentary sovereignty: the legislature above all other organs.
correctChoice: External sovereignty: final authority in relation to other states.
explanation: External sovereignty is final authority towards other states, free from outside interference. Internal sovereignty concerns authority within the state, which is the near-miss here.

subject: International Law
stem: A constitution begins with 'We, the people' and says that all public authority comes from the people. Which source of sovereignty does this show?
choice1: Popular sovereignty.
choice2: National sovereignty.
choice3: Royal sovereignty.
choice4: Parliamentary sovereignty.
correctChoice: Popular sovereignty.
explanation: Popular sovereignty places final authority in the people themselves, who may act through representatives. National sovereignty attributes it to the nation as an abstract unit, which is close but not what the wording says.

subject: International Law
stem: A constitution says that sovereignty belongs to the nationalities and peoples of the state, and that each of them is also a constituent territorial unit. Which combination is present?
choice1: National sovereignty with elements of state or provincial sovereignty.
choice2: National sovereignty with elements of pluralistic royal sovereignty.
choice3: Parliamentary sovereignty with elements of popular sovereignty.
choice4: Pluralistic sovereignty shifting between monarch and parliament.
correctChoice: National sovereignty with elements of state or provincial sovereignty.
explanation: Giving sovereignty to nationalities and peoples points to national sovereignty. Treating those groups as territorial units adds a state or provincial element, which is typical of federations.

subject: International Law
stem: A constitution says that all authority comes from the monarch, who is the final source of legislative, executive and judicial power. This shows:
choice1: royal sovereignty.
choice2: popular sovereignty.
choice3: national sovereignty.
choice4: pluralistic sovereignty.
correctChoice: royal sovereignty.
explanation: Royal sovereignty places final authority in the monarch. This differs from a constitutional monarchy built on popular sovereignty, where the monarch holds only constituted powers.

subject: International Law
stem: Which description fits pluralistic sovereignty?
choice1: Final authority moves between different actors instead of staying with one.
choice2: Final authority is split equally between the three branches of the state.
choice3: Final authority belongs to the people but is used only through referenda.
choice4: Final authority belongs to whichever court decides the case last.
correctChoice: Final authority moves between different actors instead of staying with one.
explanation: Pluralistic sovereignty means the ultimate source of authority shifts between actors, rather than resting permanently with the people, the monarch, parliament or the units.

subject: International Law
stem: What is the main reason for dividing public power into separate branches?
choice1: To stop power from concentrating and to prevent the abuse that follows.
choice2: To make the work of the three branches faster, cheaper and more efficient.
choice3: To place the judiciary in a position of control over the other two branches.
choice4: To make the constitutional rules that limit the use of public power unnecessary.
correctChoice: To stop power from concentrating and to prevent the abuse that follows.
explanation: Separation is a means to an end: dividing functions limits power and so protects freedoms. Concentrated power may be efficient, but it invites abuse.

subject: International Law
stem: A constitution says that no member of parliament may at the same time hold judicial office. Which aspect of the separation of powers is this?
choice1: Personal separation: the same individual may not staff two branches.
choice2: Institutional separation: separate organs carry out separate functions.
choice3: Functional separation: authority is divided into three kinds of function.
choice4: Vertical separation: power is divided between the levels of the state.
correctChoice: Personal separation: the same individual may not staff two branches.
explanation: Functional separation divides authority into functions; institutional separation gives them to different organs; personal separation keeps the staff of the branches apart. A ban on holding two offices is personal.

subject: International Law
stem: The idea that public authority can be divided into legislative, executive and judicial functions is which aspect of the separation of powers?
choice1: Functional separation: authority is divided into three kinds of function.
choice2: Institutional separation: separate organs carry out separate functions.
choice3: Personal separation: the same individual may not staff two branches.
choice4: Vertical separation: power is divided between the levels of the state.
correctChoice: Functional separation: authority is divided into three kinds of function.
explanation: Functional separation is the division of authority into three functions. Allocating those functions to distinct organs is institutional, and keeping the staff apart is personal.

subject: International Law
stem: What does the pure doctrine of the separation of powers require?
choice1: Each branch keeps its own function, does not encroach on the others and has its own staff.
choice2: Each branch keeps its own function, but the same people may serve in more than one branch.
choice3: The legislature supervises the other branches, which act on authority delegated to them.
choice4: A single organ holds the three functions but is divided internally into three sections.
correctChoice: Each branch keeps its own function, does not encroach on the others and has its own staff.
explanation: The pure doctrine demands three branches, three functions, no encroachment and separate personnel. Allowing shared membership drops the personal element and is the near-miss.

subject: International Law
stem: How do checks and balances relate to the separation of powers?
choice1: They complete separation by giving each branch ways of controlling the others.
choice2: They replace separation in those states that do not divide power into functions.
choice3: They are simply another name for the personal dimension of the separation of powers.
choice4: They apply only to the relationship between the central level and the regional level.
correctChoice: They complete separation by giving each branch ways of controlling the others.
explanation: Separation allocates the functions; checks and balances supply the mutual controls. The two devices work together rather than one replacing the other.

subject: International Law
stem: In constitutional design, the separation of powers is best described as:
choice1: a means to limit power and so protect individual and collective freedoms.
choice2: an end in itself, whatever it may produce for the freedoms of the citizens.
choice3: a rule of political practice that carries no legal force before any court.
choice4: a technique for making the decisions of government faster and cheaper.
correctChoice: a means to limit power and so protect individual and collective freedoms.
explanation: The chain runs from separating power, to limiting it by constitutional rules, to protecting freedoms. Separation is instrumental, not a goal in its own right.

subject: International Law
stem: A constitution shares legislative, executive and judicial power between the union, the regions and self-administered areas. Which dimension is this?
choice1: Vertical separation: power is shared between the levels of the state.
choice2: Horizontal separation: power is shared between branches at one level.
choice3: Personal separation: the same individual may not staff two branches.
choice4: Functional separation: authority is divided into three kinds of function.
correctChoice: Vertical separation: power is shared between the levels of the state.
explanation: Horizontal separation operates between legislature, executive and judiciary at the same level. Sharing power between central, regional and local levels is vertical.

subject: International Law
stem: A constitution says the three branches are separated 'to the extent possible'. What is the main risk of this wording?
choice1: It is vague enough to excuse a failure to keep the branches separate.
choice2: It makes the provision binding on private parties as well as the state.
choice3: It turns the horizontal separation of powers into a vertical one.
choice4: It makes every piece of delegated legislation unconstitutional.
correctChoice: It is vague enough to excuse a failure to keep the branches separate.
explanation: Such wording can be read as useful flexibility, for example in an emergency, but it is open enough to be used as an excuse for dropping separation and mutual control.

subject: International Law
stem: A constitutional article on the structure of government is declared 'descriptive only and non-justiciable'. What follows?
choice1: Its terms cannot be used as the basis of a claim before a court.
choice2: Its terms bind the courts but place no duty on the legislature.
choice3: Its terms may be enforced only by the head of state in person.
choice4: Its terms lose their effect as soon as the government changes.
correctChoice: Its terms cannot be used as the basis of a claim before a court.
explanation: A non-justiciable clause cannot be relied on in litigation. It may still describe how the state is built, but it gives a court no legal basis to decide a dispute.

subject: International Law
stem: Which statement about how the separation of powers works in practice is most accurate?
choice1: Separation is never perfect, and some overlap between branches can be justified.
choice2: Separation is perfect in every state that has adopted a codified constitution.
choice3: Any overlap of functions between the branches produces a constitutional crisis.
choice4: Overlap between the branches is acceptable only where the constitution is uncodified.
correctChoice: Separation is never perfect, and some overlap between branches can be justified.
explanation: Separation operates differently from state to state and always involves cooperation. Some overlap is justified; what varies is how strictly a constitution controls it.

subject: International Law
stem: A head of state bans public gatherings by emergency decree and allows detention without access to a court, saying this protects the public. For constitutionalism, what is the decisive question?
choice1: Whether the power has a legal basis, legal limits and is open to review.
choice2: Whether the head of state sincerely believes the public is being protected.
choice3: Whether most of the population supports the measure that was taken.
choice4: Whether the decree was put in writing and published in the proper form.
correctChoice: Whether the power has a legal basis, legal limits and is open to review.
explanation: Constitutionalism asks what stops a government from doing whatever it wants. A good purpose is not enough: the power must be conferred by law, limited by law and reviewable.

subject: International Law
stem: Why does a constitution matter for the protection of human rights?
choice1: It places limits and duties on public authorities and opens ways to influence politics.
choice2: It transfers the whole task of protecting rights to international courts and treaty bodies.
choice3: It makes every constitutional right absolute, so that no restriction can ever be lawful.
choice4: It leaves the scope of each right to the discretion of the executive of the day.
correctChoice: It places limits and duties on public authorities and opens ways to influence politics.
explanation: Constitutions limit and bind public authorities in their dealings with people and create channels for participation. That is what prevents absolute power, even though rights may still be restricted lawfully.

subject: International Law
stem: Why is 'parliament' not simply another word for 'legislature'?
choice1: The legislature is the power to make law, and bodies other than parliament may share in it.
choice2: Parliament is the power to make law, and the legislature is the body that scrutinises it.
choice3: The legislature exists only in federal states, while parliament exists in unitary states.
choice4: Parliament forms part of the executive branch in every parliamentary system.
correctChoice: The legislature is the power to make law, and bodies other than parliament may share in it.
explanation: The legislature is the lawmaking power; parliament is an institution that normally takes part in it, often together with the executive or head of state. One wrong option swaps the two terms.

subject: International Law
stem: Which three tasks are traditionally given to parliament?
choice1: Legislation, scrutiny and representation.
choice2: Legislation, representation and adjudication.
choice3: Representation, prosecution and budgeting.
choice4: Scrutiny, adjudication and foreign policy.
correctChoice: Legislation, scrutiny and representation.
explanation: Parliament makes binding decisions for citizens, checks the other institutions on their behalf, and represents the people. Adjudication and administration belong to the other branches.

subject: International Law
stem: A statute allows a minister to adopt detailed rules that implement it. How is the minister's instrument best classified?
choice1: Delegated legislation, made by the executive under a power given by statute.
choice2: Primary legislation, because the rules bind citizens in exactly the same way.
choice3: A legislative reserve, because the statute keeps the subject matter for itself.
choice4: A non-binding guideline, because parliament itself did not vote on the text.
correctChoice: Delegated legislation, made by the executive under a power given by statute.
explanation: Primary legislation is adopted by the legislature; delegated legislation is adopted by executive bodies inside limits the legislature sets. A legislative reserve is the opposite device: it blocks delegation.

subject: International Law
stem: What does a legislative reserve do in a constitution?
choice1: It marks subjects the legislature must regulate itself and cannot delegate away.
choice2: It marks subjects the executive may regulate without any statutory basis.
choice3: It keeps a fixed number of parliamentary seats for the governing parties.
choice4: It lets the executive legislate during the period when parliament is dissolved.
correctChoice: It marks subjects the legislature must regulate itself and cannot delegate away.
explanation: A legislative reserve protects certain subject matter for the legislature, so the executive cannot deal with it by delegated instruments. One wrong option states the exact reverse.

subject: International Law
stem: Which set of powers describes parliament's ability to check the executive?
choice1: Rights to information and investigation, control of the budget, and lawmaking.
choice2: Rights to prosecute ministers, to appoint the judges and to annul their rulings.
choice3: Powers to issue decrees, to declare an emergency and to dissolve itself at will.
choice4: Powers to interpret the constitution and to annul statutes that conflict with it.
correctChoice: Rights to information and investigation, control of the budget, and lawmaking.
explanation: Parliament finds out what the executive does (information), inquires into it (investigation), holds the power of the purse, and sets the legal framework. Annulling statutes is a task for courts.

subject: International Law
stem: What is the essential difference between representative and direct democracy?
choice1: Elected members take binding decisions for citizens; in direct democracy citizens decide themselves.
choice2: Citizens take the decisions themselves; in direct democracy they elect members to decide for them.
choice3: Representative democracy suits federal states, while direct democracy suits unitary states.
choice4: Direct democracy works entirely without elections of any kind taking place.
correctChoice: Elected members take binding decisions for citizens; in direct democracy citizens decide themselves.
explanation: Representative democracy rests on elected people deciding for citizens; direct democracy lets citizens decide. One wrong option simply swaps the two definitions.

subject: International Law
stem: Which activity is typical of the executive branch?
choice1: Carrying out policy and legislation and conducting foreign policy and defence.
choice2: Deciding whether a statute is constitutional in a dispute between two parties.
choice3: Approving the budget and fixing how much money the state is allowed to spend.
choice4: Fixing the rank of each type of norm inside the hierarchy of the legal order.
correctChoice: Carrying out policy and legislation and conducting foreign policy and defence.
explanation: The executive runs the daily affairs of the state: it proposes priorities, implements law and policy, conducts external relations and defence, and spends the budget within parliament's limits.

subject: International Law
stem: How is responsibility for the state budget normally divided?
choice1: Parliament approves the budget and sets the limits; the executive spends it.
choice2: The executive approves the budget and sets the limits; parliament spends it.
choice3: Both branches draw on the budget independently and without coordination.
choice4: The courts approve the budget before either of the branches may use it.
correctChoice: Parliament approves the budget and sets the limits; the executive spends it.
explanation: The power of the purse belongs to parliament, which decides how much may be spent and on what. The executive prepares and executes spending. One wrong option reverses the two roles.

subject: International Law
stem: During an emergency, a constitution lets the government adopt measures with the force of legislation. What is the best analysis?
choice1: Functional separation survives, but personal separation weakens, as one actor does both.
choice2: Personal separation survives, but functional separation disappears while the emergency lasts.
choice3: The separation of powers is suspended completely until the emergency has ended.
choice4: The measures are void, because only parliament may ever adopt binding legislation.
correctChoice: Functional separation survives, but personal separation weakens, as one actor does both.
explanation: The legislative function still exists; what changes is that the people exercising the executive function also exercise it. That weakens personal separation, not functional separation.

subject: International Law
stem: Which task belongs to the judiciary?
choice1: Interpreting legislation and reviewing the lawfulness of acts of public authorities.
choice2: Setting the political agenda and the legislative priorities of the state for the year.
choice3: Deciding the level of taxation and approving the spending of public money each year.
choice4: Representing the state in negotiations with other states and with organisations.
correctChoice: Interpreting legislation and reviewing the lawfulness of acts of public authorities.
explanation: Courts interpret legislation, review the lawfulness and sometimes the constitutionality of measures, check compliance with treaty obligations, and protect rights.

subject: International Law
stem: Judicial review is best defined as a procedure in which:
choice1: a court tests a decision, act or norm of a public body against a higher norm.
choice2: a higher court re-examines the facts that a lower court found in the case.
choice3: parliament examines whether a court has applied a statute in the right way.
choice4: the executive examines whether a statute should be repealed or amended.
correctChoice: a court tests a decision, act or norm of a public body against a higher norm.
explanation: Judicial review measures a measure against a higher norm, usually the constitution. It is not an appeal on the facts, which is the near-miss here.

subject: International Law
stem: Two valid rules conflict: one is higher in rank, the other is more specific. Which conflict rule is applied first?
choice1: Lex superior: the higher-ranking norm comes first.
choice2: Lex specialis: the more specific norm comes first.
choice3: Lex posterior: the more recent norm comes first.
choice4: Neither: both conflicting norms lose validity.
correctChoice: Lex superior: the higher-ranking norm comes first.
explanation: The usual order is lex superior, then lex specialis, then lex posterior. Rank is settled before specificity, and specificity before date.

subject: International Law
stem: A constitutional court examines a bill before it enters into force. This illustrates:
choice1: ex ante review, because the examination happens before entry into force.
choice2: ex post review, because parliament has already voted on the text of the bill.
choice3: concrete review, because one specific legislative text is being examined.
choice4: decentralised review, because no ordinary court has been involved so far.
correctChoice: ex ante review, because the examination happens before entry into force.
explanation: Ex ante review looks at a text before it enters into force; ex post review looks at measures already adopted. Whether a real dispute exists is the separate concrete/abstract question.

subject: International Law
stem: Why is ex post review more common than ex ante review?
choice1: Checking every bill in advance would be slow, so review waits until a conflict appears.
choice2: Checking bills before they enter into force is forbidden in almost every constitution.
choice3: Only review after entry into force may be carried out by a court rather than a minister.
choice4: Review before entry into force may be requested only by the executive branch.
correctChoice: Checking every bill in advance would be slow, so review waits until a conflict appears.
explanation: Given the number of bills and the time review takes, most systems wait until a real problem arises. Worries about giving unelected judges too large a role point the same way.

subject: International Law
stem: A court hearing a live dispute asks whether the statute it is about to apply is constitutional. This is:
choice1: concrete review, because a real dispute before a court gave rise to it.
choice2: abstract review, because the court weighs the statute in general terms.
choice3: ex ante review, because the statute was not yet applied to the parties.
choice4: centralised review, because only one court may raise such a question.
correctChoice: concrete review, because a real dispute before a court gave rise to it.
explanation: Concrete review grows out of an actual dispute. Abstract review is not linked to a live case, for example when an opposition challenges a statute on its own initiative.

subject: International Law
stem: A parliamentary opposition asks the constitutional court to examine a new statute although nobody has yet been affected by it. This is:
choice1: abstract review, because no real dispute lies behind the challenge.
choice2: concrete review, because one specific statute is being challenged.
choice3: ex ante review, because the statute has not been applied to anyone.
choice4: decentralised review, because the applicant is not itself a court.
correctChoice: abstract review, because no real dispute lies behind the challenge.
explanation: Abstract review is review that is not occasioned by a live court dispute. Whether the statute is already in force is the separate ex ante / ex post question.

subject: International Law
stem: In a centralised system of constitutional review:
choice1: only one designated or specialised court may review the constitutionality of statutes.
choice2: every court may review constitutionality, with the highest court having the last word.
choice3: a parliamentary committee, rather than a court, decides on constitutionality.
choice4: review may take place only before the statute has entered into force.
correctChoice: only one designated or specialised court may review the constitutionality of statutes.
explanation: Centralised review concentrates the power in one body, such as a constitutional or supreme court. Letting all courts review, subject to the highest court, describes the decentralised model.

subject: International Law
stem: Which observation about decentralised constitutional review is accurate?
choice1: All courts may review, yet statutes are set aside less often than in centralised systems.
choice2: All courts may review, and statutes are therefore set aside more often than elsewhere.
choice3: Only the highest court may review, and its rulings bind every lower court in the state.
choice4: Courts may review only in proceedings where no live dispute between parties exists.
correctChoice: All courts may review, yet statutes are set aside less often than in centralised systems.
explanation: Decentralised systems open review to all courts but in practice produce fewer findings of unconstitutionality. The highest court still has the final word and precedent does much of the work.

subject: International Law
stem: A court finds a statute incompatible with the constitution and refuses to apply it in the case, but the statute stays on the statute book. This is:
choice1: disapplication, because the statute still exists but is not applied here.
choice2: annulment, because the statute has lost its legal effect for everyone.
choice3: abstract review, because no live dispute was needed for the ruling.
choice4: ex ante review, because the statute never properly entered into force.
correctChoice: disapplication, because the statute still exists but is not applied here.
explanation: Disapplication leaves the statute in existence but unused in that case. Annulment removes it from the legal order altogether.

subject: International Law
stem: What follows from the annulment of an unconstitutional statute?
choice1: The statute ceases to exist and nobody may apply it any longer.
choice2: The statute stays in force but is set aside in the individual case.
choice3: The statute returns to parliament for one further and final vote.
choice4: The statute is suspended until the next parliamentary election.
correctChoice: The statute ceases to exist and nobody may apply it any longer.
explanation: Annulment abolishes the statute. Setting it aside only in the case at hand is the milder outcome, disapplication.

subject: International Law
stem: Which of the following is an argument against judicial review of legislation?
choice1: Judges are not elected, so they should not refuse to apply the will of parliament.
choice2: Judges are professionals and less driven by party politics than legislators are.
choice3: Review protects the place of the constitution at the top of the hierarchy of norms.
choice4: Review supplies a check on lawmakers that protects minorities and human rights.
correctChoice: Judges are not elected, so they should not refuse to apply the will of parliament.
explanation: The democratic objection stresses that judges are unelected and are meant to apply law rather than make it. The other three options are the standard arguments in favour.

subject: International Law
stem: Which feature is typical of a presidential system?
choice1: The president is elected for a fixed term and does not need parliament's confidence.
choice2: The president is elected by parliament for a fixed term and may be dismissed by it.
choice3: The president appoints a prime minister who answers to parliament and not to them.
choice4: The president holds ceremonial duties only while the cabinet runs the government.
correctChoice: The president is elected for a fixed term and does not need parliament's confidence.
explanation: In a presidential system the president heads the government, has a fixed term and cannot be removed by a vote of no confidence, although impeachment stays possible.

subject: International Law
stem: What is the decisive criterion for calling a system parliamentary rather than presidential?
choice1: Whether parliament can dismiss the government.
choice2: Whether the head of state is a monarch or president.
choice3: Whether the head of government is elected directly.
choice4: Whether parliament has one chamber or two chambers.
correctChoice: Whether parliament can dismiss the government.
explanation: The key question is political accountability: if parliament can dismiss the government, the system is parliamentary. The form of the headship of state and the shape of the legislature are separate issues.

subject: International Law
stem: Which arrangement is typical of a semi-presidential system?
choice1: A directly elected president is head of state and a prime minister leads the government.
choice2: A monarch is head of state while a directly elected president leads the government for a term.
choice3: One president is both head of state and head of government, with no prime minister at all.
choice4: Parliament exercises the executive function itself, so there is no separate government.
correctChoice: A directly elected president is head of state and a prime minister leads the government.
explanation: Semi-presidentialism combines a popularly elected president as head of state with a prime minister leading the government, so executive power is shared and parliament keeps influence.

subject: International Law
subtopic: Head of state and head of government
stem: In a parliamentary system, how are the two headships usually arranged?
choice1: A president or monarch is head of state; a prime minister is head of government.
choice2: One single officeholder is head of state and head of government at the same time.
choice3: Parliament acts as the head of state and the cabinet acts as head of government.
choice4: The president of the constitutional court acts as the head of state of the republic.
correctChoice: A president or monarch is head of state; a prime minister is head of government.
explanation: Parliamentary and semi-presidential systems split the ceremonial headship of state from the political leadership of the government. Combining the two is the presidential model.

subject: International Law
stem: Which statement about the headship of state is correct?
choice1: In some systems a collective body, not one person, performs head-of-state functions.
choice2: Every state must designate exactly one natural person as the holder of that office.
choice3: A collective head of state is impossible in a republic, though a monarchy may have one.
choice4: Only monarchies may share head-of-state functions between two or more individuals.
correctChoice: In some systems a collective body, not one person, performs head-of-state functions.
explanation: Some constitutions give head-of-state functions, including external representation, to a collegiate body rather than to an individual.

subject: International Law
stem: In a republican parliamentary system built on popular sovereignty, how is the head of government usually installed?
choice1: Parliament elects the candidate first, and formal appointment follows afterwards.
choice2: The head of state appoints the candidate first, and parliament may then reject them.
choice3: The outgoing head of government names a successor, who is confirmed by a court.
choice4: The electorate chooses the head of government in a separate national ballot.
correctChoice: Parliament elects the candidate first, and formal appointment follows afterwards.
explanation: Where sovereignty is popular and the state a republic, parliament normally elects the candidate before formal appointment. Appointment first, with parliament only able to object, is the pattern of some constitutional monarchies.

subject: International Law
stem: A constitution says that decrees of the head of state take effect only if a minister also signs them. What is the main purpose?
choice1: The head of state cannot act alone, and political responsibility passes to the government.
choice2: The government cannot act alone, and political responsibility passes to the head of state.
choice3: The head of state gains a veto over the policy decisions of the government.
choice4: The decree is certified as being in conformity with the constitution.
correctChoice: The head of state cannot act alone, and political responsibility passes to the government.
explanation: Countersignature stops the head of state from governing alone and shifts responsibility to the minister or head of government, which protects the neutral position of the head of state. One option reverses this.

subject: International Law
stem: How does impeachment differ from a vote of no confidence?
choice1: Impeachment is a legal process about serious wrongdoing; no confidence is political disapproval.
choice2: Impeachment is political disapproval; a vote of no confidence is a criminal trial of a minister.
choice3: Impeachment is used only against ministers, and no confidence only against the head of state.
choice4: Impeachment requires a referendum, while a vote of no confidence requires a court judgment.
correctChoice: Impeachment is a legal process about serious wrongdoing; no confidence is political disapproval.
explanation: Impeachment responds to serious misconduct and resembles a prosecution, usually of the head of state. A vote of no confidence is a political tool of parliamentary systems. One option swaps them.

subject: International Law
stem: Why can a president normally not dissolve the legislature in a presidential system?
choice1: The two branches receive their mandates separately and survive independently of each other.
choice2: Dissolution belongs to the constitutional court in every presidential system of government.
choice3: Presidential systems always have a single chamber, which cannot be dissolved early.
choice4: Dissolution is possible only in states whose constitution is uncodified.
correctChoice: The two branches receive their mandates separately and survive independently of each other.
explanation: Separate origin and separate survival mean the president cannot end parliament's term. Where dissolution exists at all, constitutions usually limit how and how often it may be used.

subject: International Law
stem: Voters cast their ballots for the candidates themselves rather than for intermediaries who vote on their behalf. Which election principle is this?
choice1: Directness of the vote.
choice2: Freedom of the vote.
choice3: Equality of the vote.
choice4: Secrecy of the vote.
correctChoice: Directness of the vote.
explanation: Directness means the vote goes to the contestants themselves. Freedom concerns the voter's choice, equality the 'one person, one vote' rule, and secrecy the protection of the ballot.

subject: International Law
stem: Under first past the post, what does a candidate need in order to win the seat?
choice1: More votes than any other candidate, however small the share.
choice2: More than half of all the valid votes cast in the constituency.
choice3: A share of the seats equal to the party's national vote share.
choice4: Two thirds of the votes cast in the constituency concerned.
correctChoice: More votes than any other candidate, however small the share.
explanation: First past the post needs only one vote more than the nearest rival. Requiring more than half the votes, often with a second round, is the absolute majority system.

subject: International Law
stem: What is the defining feature of proportional representation?
choice1: Seats are shared out in proportion to the votes each party receives.
choice2: The candidate with most votes in a district takes that district's seat.
choice3: Seats are divided equally between all the parties that stand.
choice4: Only parties with more than half of the votes receive any seats.
correctChoice: Seats are shared out in proportion to the votes each party receives.
explanation: Proportional representation allocates seats by vote share, so roughly twenty per cent of the votes gives roughly twenty per cent of the seats.

subject: International Law
stem: What is the usual criticism of a closed list system of proportional representation?
choice1: Voters choose a party but have little say over which individuals take its seats.
choice2: Voters choose individuals but have little say over the balance between parties.
choice3: Votes cast for the smaller parties are wasted more often than in other systems.
choice4: Voters must rank every candidate who appears on the ballot paper in order.
correctChoice: Voters choose a party but have little say over which individuals take its seats.
explanation: The party fills its seats from a list fixed in advance, so voters have limited influence over who is elected. Some systems soften this with preference votes.

subject: International Law
stem: Which description fits the single transferable vote?
choice1: Voters rank the candidates and the rankings are used to allocate the seats.
choice2: Voters cast one vote for a party list that the party fills in a fixed order.
choice3: Voters cast two votes, one for a candidate and one for a party list.
choice4: The candidate with most first preferences takes every seat in the district.
correctChoice: Voters rank the candidates and the rankings are used to allocate the seats.
explanation: Under the single transferable vote, voters rank candidates and preferences are transferred when seats are allocated. Two votes, one personal and one for a list, describes a mixed member system.

subject: International Law
stem: Which effect is commonly linked to single-member constituencies?
choice1: A move towards two large parties, because voters avoid wasting their vote.
choice2: A move towards many small parties, so broad coalitions become necessary.
choice3: The loss of any personal link between voters and their representative.
choice4: Seat shares that closely mirror the national vote share of each party.
correctChoice: A move towards two large parties, because voters avoid wasting their vote.
explanation: Single-member districts create a close link between representative and voters, but encourage tactical voting for the bigger parties, which concentrates the party system.

subject: International Law
stem: What is the main justification for a bicameral parliament?
choice1: It slows down hasty decisions and checks the majority in the first chamber.
choice2: It makes the adoption of legislation faster than in a single-chamber parliament.
choice3: It moves the power to make legislation from parliament towards the executive.
choice4: It makes judicial review of legislation unnecessary in almost every situation.
correctChoice: It slows down hasty decisions and checks the majority in the first chamber.
explanation: A second chamber adds delay and a check on the majority. In federal states it also represents the units; in unitary states it is usually a chamber of reflection.

subject: International Law
stem: What is meant by perfect bicameralism?
choice1: Both chambers hold the same rights of initiative, amendment and veto.
choice2: Both chambers are elected directly by the same voters on the same day.
choice3: The second chamber may delay a bill but can never block it entirely.
choice4: The two chambers always sit and vote together as a single assembly.
correctChoice: Both chambers hold the same rights of initiative, amendment and veto.
